course.title: Small Buildings and Architectural Design
course.description: How a small building is designed and drawn: site, programme, structure, light, heat and the drawings that describe it.
course.audience: Adults with school maths and physics who have not studied architecture.

paragraphs: A wall 6 m high at latitude 52 degrees north throws a noon shadow 3.3 m long in June and 23.1 m long in December, and a list of rooms that adds up to 68 m² needs a house of about 80 m² once the walls, the hall and the services are counted. Small buildings are designed with numbers of this kind, and most of them come from school mathematics, such as the tangent of an angle or a single division. Architectural design is the work of deciding where a building stands, what spaces it holds and how it is put together, and for a small building nearly every one of those decisions can be checked on paper before anything is built.

Knowing those numbers changes what you see in buildings you already know. A room that is gloomy at the back is too deep for the height of its window, a window that runs with water on a winter morning is colder than the dew point of the air beside it, and a stair that feels steep has steps whose height and depth break a rule usually credited to a 17th-century French architect. With a drawing at a known scale and a calculator you can find faults like these before they are built, and work out which change would put each one right while the building is still on paper.
outcomes: You'll be able to read a site and place a building by sun.
You'll be able to read plan, section and elevation and use scale.
You'll be able to compute a stair, a joist moment and a U-value.
You'll be able to judge light, condensation and comfort.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on Geometry: Shape and Space, Engineering: Structures and Machines, Physics: Motion and Forces.

modules.title: Site, brief and drawings
modules.description: Reading a place, turning needs into area, and the three views.

modules.title: Making space
modules.description: Moving through a building, holding it up and lighting it.

modules.title: Heat, moisture and weather
modules.description: U-values, airtightness, condensation, comfort and roofs.

modules.title: Drawing it together
modules.description: The drawing set and a worked small building.

concepts.title: Noon sun altitude
concepts.summary: At noon the sun's altitude is 90 degrees minus latitude plus declination; the declination is +23.44 at June solstice and -23.44 at December solstice.

concepts.title: Orientation
concepts.summary: In the northern hemisphere the south face receives low winter sun and, with shading, little summer sun.

concepts.title: Programme
concepts.summary: The list of spaces a building must provide, with areas, relationships and requirements.

concepts.title: Net to gross
concepts.summary: Net area is room floor area; gross area adds walls, corridors and services, so gross = net / efficiency.

concepts.title: Plan
concepts.summary: A horizontal cut about 1.2 m above the floor, looking down.

concepts.title: Section and elevation
concepts.summary: A section is a vertical cut seen from the side; an elevation is a view of an outside face without a cut.

concepts.title: Scale
concepts.summary: 1:50 means 1 unit on paper stands for 50 in the building.

concepts.title: Stair rule
concepts.summary: Riser R and going G satisfy 2R + G between 550 and 700 mm; about 630 mm is comfortable.

concepts.title: Circulation
concepts.summary: The space people use to get between rooms: halls, corridors, stairs.

concepts.title: Load path
concepts.summary: The continuous route by which loads travel from roof and floors through members to the ground.

concepts.title: Floor load
concepts.summary: A residential floor carries dead load (self-weight, finishes) and imposed load (people, furniture), combined with factors 1.35 and 1.5 for strength checks.

concepts.title: Daylight factor
concepts.summary: Indoor illuminance as a percentage of the unobstructed outdoor illuminance under an overcast sky.

concepts.title: Depth rule
concepts.summary: A side-lit room is adequately lit near the back if L/W + L/Hw is no more than 2/(1-R) for average surface reflectance R.

concepts.title: Thermal resistance
concepts.summary: R = thickness / conductivity (m^2 K/W) for a layer; resistances in series add.

concepts.title: U-value
concepts.summary: U = 1 / (Rsi + sum of R + Rse), in W/m^2 K; heat loss Q = U A dT.

concepts.title: Ventilation heat loss
concepts.summary: H = 0.33 n V in W/K for n air changes per hour and V in m^3.

concepts.title: Dew point
concepts.summary: The temperature at which air of a given moisture content becomes saturated, so water condenses on any colder surface.

concepts.title: Comfort factors
concepts.summary: Air temperature, radiant temperature, air speed, humidity, clothing and activity together set comfort.

concepts.title: Passive design
concepts.summary: Using form, orientation, glazing, mass and ventilation to keep comfort with little energy.

concepts.title: Pitch
concepts.summary: The roof slope angle, rise over half the span.

concepts.title: Rainfall run-off
concepts.summary: Flow Q = i A, rainfall intensity times plan area.

concepts.title: Drawing set
concepts.summary: Site plan, floor plans, sections, elevations and details, each at a scale suited to what it must show.

concepts.title: Conventions
concepts.summary: Line weights, symbols, grid, dimensions and north arrow so the reader can build without asking.

concepts.title: Synthesis
concepts.summary: Each decision affects the others; check them against the brief.

concepts.title: Fabric first
concepts.summary: Reduce heat loss through the envelope before adding systems.

lessons.title: Reading a site: sun, wind and ground

lead.text: The **sun** crosses the plot on a path that depends on the season; the prevailing **wind** arrives from one quarter more than the others; the **slope** decides where water runs and what must be dug or built up; the road and the neighbours decide where people come from and who can see in.

The order in which they are noted therefore matters: a designer who fixes the plan first has to fight the site afterwards, while one who reads the site first can place the long walls, the entrance and the garden where the site already helps.

diagram.alt: A site plan with north at the top, dashed contour lines, three trees, a neighbouring building to the east, a road along the south edge and an arrow showing the prevailing wind from the south-west. The second view adds a building footprint with its long side facing south.
diagram.caption: A site is the plot plus everything acting on it. The second view puts the footprint where the sun, the wind and the trees allow it.

reveal.text: At 21 June the sun at that latitude rises about 50 degrees away from north, towards the north-east, and sets in the north-west. The next screen shows why.

lead.text: Earth’s axis keeps pointing at the same spot in the sky while Earth travels round the sun, so in June the Northern Hemisphere leans towards the sun and in December it leans away. The sun is then directly overhead at a place 23.44 degrees north of the equator in June and 23.44 degrees south of it in December. That angle, measured from the equator to the latitude where the sun is overhead at noon, is the sun’s **declination**, and it is +23.44 at the June solstice, −23.44 at the December solstice and 0 at the two **equinoxes**.

The height of the sun above the horizon, measured as an angle, is its **altitude**. At noon the sun stands due south in the Northern Hemisphere, and its altitude is the equinox value, 90 degrees minus your latitude, shifted by the declination: **altitude = 90° − latitude + declination**. At latitude 52 this gives 90 − 52 + 23.44 = 61.4 degrees in June, 90 − 52 = 38 at the equinoxes and 90 − 52 − 23.44 = 14.6 in December.

afterFigure.text: Because the sun swings between 14.6 and 61.4 degrees in one year, the same wall gets very different sun at different dates, and this is also the reason the sun rises due east only at the equinoxes: on any other date the declination moves the whole path north or south of east.

steps.headline: Find the noon altitude at latitude 52 degrees north on 21 June, and then on 21 December.

workedSteps.text: The equinox altitude comes from the latitude alone, because the declination there is zero.
In June the declination is +23.44, so the sun stands higher than at the equinox.
In December the declination is −23.44, so the same sum gives a lower sun.
The difference between the two is twice the tilt, which is why the swing is so large.

reveal.text: The neighbour's wall throws a shadow about 12 m long at noon in December, and the gap is only 8 m, so your wall is shaded up to 2.0 m. The same low sun that makes long shadows is the one you want indoors, so what stands to the south matters as much as the glass.

lead.text: A wall and its shadow, with the sun ray joining the top of the wall to the tip of the shadow, form a right-angled triangle. The altitude is the angle at the tip, the wall is the side opposite it and the shadow is the side beside it, and since tan(angle) = opposite ÷ adjacent, **tan(altitude) = height ÷ shadow**. Rearranging gives **shadow = height ÷ tan(altitude)**.

For the 6 m wall at latitude 52, the June altitude of 61.4 degrees gives 6 ÷ tan 61.4° = 3.3 m, the equinox altitude of 38 degrees gives 7.7 m, and the December altitude of 14.6 degrees gives 6 ÷ 0.2603 = 23.1 m. The height has not changed, but the shadow in December is seven times as long as in June.

afterFigure.text: A neighbour’s 6 m wall to the south would put the whole of a 20 m garden in shade at noon in midwinter.

steps.headline: A 9 m wall stands at latitude 50 degrees north. Find the length of its noon shadow on 21 December.

workedSteps.text: The equinox altitude is 90 minus the latitude.
In December the declination is −23.44, so the altitude is
The wall and its shadow are the two shorter sides of a right-angled triangle, and the altitude is the angle at the tip of the shadow.

lead.text: The same triangle explains why south glass is not simply “warmest”. In June the sun is high, so an overhang that projects 0.6 m casts a shadow 0.6 × tan 61.4° = 1.10 m down the wall, deep enough to cover all but the bottom 0.1 m of a window whose head is 0.3 m below the overhang and whose sill is 1.2 m below it. In December the altitude is 14.6 degrees, so the shadow is 0.6 × tan 14.6° = 0.16 m, and the whole window is in sun.

Unshaded, south glass lets in a great deal of sun in summer, when the heat is not wanted, as well as in winter, when it is. The orientation that suits heating therefore needs *shading*, and the winter sun is the one that matters for heating, because it arrives when the building loses heat fastest.

afterFigure.text: The overhang’s depth and its height above the window set how much of each season’s sun passes.

diagram.alt: A section through a south wall with a window and a 0.6 metre overhang above it. In June the noon sun ray is steep and the overhang's shadow reaches 1.10 metres down the wall, covering the window. In December the ray is shallow and the shadow reaches only 0.16 metres, so the window is in sun.

lead.text: The formula was written for the Northern Hemisphere, where the noon sun is in the south.

reveal.text: Below the equator the roles swap: the June sun is the low winter sun, 31.6 degrees at noon at 35 degrees south, and the December sun is high at 78.4 degrees.

blocks.text: At latitude 52 degrees north, the noon sun on 21 June stands 61.4 degrees above the horizon, and on 21 December only 14.6 degrees. A 6 m wall throws a shadow 3.3 m long in the first case and 23.1 m long in the second, so the same plot is a sunny garden in summer and a shadowed strip in winter.
Both angles follow from the latitude and the date alone, so they are known before anything is built.

intro.promise: By the end you’ll be able to compute the noon sun altitude and a shadow length for a latitude and use them to place walls and glass.
intro.whyItMatters: The sun cannot be moved, so the placement of walls and glass either uses it or fights it.

recap.keyIdea: The noon sun altitude is 90° minus the latitude plus the declination, which is +23.44° in June, 0° at the equinoxes and −23.44° in December.

blocks.text: A shadow is the height divided by the tangent of the altitude, so the low December sun throws long shadows and the high June sun short ones. A south wall in the Northern Hemisphere collects that winter sun, and a fixed overhang shades it in summer without blocking it in winter.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson stops looking at the ground and turns a client’s brief into rooms and areas.

lessons.title: From brief to programme

lead.text: Asking a family who will live in the house, how many of them are in it at once, and what each one does between waking and sleeping produces a list of activities, and each activity needs a space. The list of spaces with the area each needs, the relationships between them and any special requirements is called the **programme**, or brief.
The areas total 68 m², and that total is the **net area**, meaning the floor inside the rooms and nothing else.

afterFigure.text: Starting from the programme keeps the question the right way round: what must happen inside, and how much floor does it need?

reveal.text: It will be more. The next screen gives the reason and the usual size of the difference.

lead.text: Rooms are separated by walls, joined by a hall, and served by a stair, a boiler cupboard and ducts, and none of that floor counts as a room. The area of the building measured to include all of it is the **gross area**. The share of the gross that is usable room is the **efficiency**, which is net ÷ gross, and for a small house a value of about 85 percent is a sensible first guess.
Rearranging the definition gives **gross = net ÷ efficiency**. For the 68 m² of rooms at 85 percent, the gross area is 68 ÷ 0.85 = 80 m², so 12 m² goes on the things that hold the rooms together.

steps.headline: Find the gross area and the build cost for 68 m² of net rooms at 85 percent efficiency and 2200 per m² of gross area.

workedSteps.text: Rearrange the definition of efficiency to find the gross area.
Substitute the net area and the efficiency written as a decimal.
Cost is charged on the whole built area, not only on the rooms.
The same budget spent on the net area alone would have under-counted the cost by 26 400.

steps.headline: A studio has 34 m² of net area at 85 percent efficiency. Find its gross area and its cost at 2200 per m².

workedSteps.text: Gross area is net divided by efficiency.
Now the cost, at 2200 per square metre.

lead.text: A double bed measures about 1.4 by 2.0 m, and a person needs to reach both long sides of it and the foot, which takes 0.7 m on each of those three sides. The bed together with that space occupies 2.8 m by 2.7 m, which is **7.56 m²**, and a 12 m² bedroom of 3.0 by 4.0 m is therefore left with 4.44 m² for a wardrobe and the door.
The same method sizes every room: list the furniture, add the clearance each piece needs to be used, and add the sums.

afterFigure.text: If you slid the bed against a wall you would lose the clearance on that side, which is why a 12 m² room is a workable double bedroom and a 9 m² one is tight.

diagram.alt: A plan of a 3 by 4 metre bedroom at 70 pixels per metre. A double bed 1.4 by 2.0 metres sits in a dashed zone 2.8 by 2.7 metres that adds 0.7 metres on both long sides and at the foot. The zone is 7.56 square metres of the room's 12.

reveal.text: Each step needs the one before it. You cannot total rooms that have no sizes, and the rate is charged on the gross area, which comes from the net.

lead.text: A bubble diagram draws each room as a circle whose area is its floor area and joins the pairs that need a direct connection. In the figure the kitchen is joined to the dining room because food travels between them many times a day, and to the store because the shopping goes there first. The bath is joined to both bedrooms and the entrance to the living room, while the bath is *not* joined to the entrance, because a bathroom door that opens on the front step is an arrangement most clients refuse.
It records the relationships so that the plan, drawn next, can be tested against them, and a plan that breaks a link has to say why.

Seven rooms are circles whose areas match their floor areas: living 18, dining 9, kitchen 10, store 3, bed 1 13, bed 2 10 and bath 5 square metres. The second view joins rooms that must be next to each other: kitchen to dining, dining to living, kitchen to store, bath to both bedrooms and the entrance to the living room.

lead.text: The 85 percent is a sensible start for a compact house, but a plan with long corridors can fall below it.

reveal.text: Plan B's gross area is 90.7 m² against 80 m² for Plan A, and the extra 10.7 m² costs 23,500 at 2200 per m². Compact plans are cheaper because less of the floor goes on getting between rooms.

blocks.text: A small two-bedroom house might need a living room of 18 m², a kitchen of 10 m², a dining area of 9 m², bedrooms of 13 and 10 m², a bathroom of 5 m² and a store of 3 m², and those seven spaces add up to 68 m². A list of this kind, naming each space the building must hold and the floor it needs, is where the design of a building begins, well before anyone draws what it will look like from outside.
The total is the floor the occupants will use inside the rooms, while the cost of the house is set by the floor area of the whole building, at a rate such as 2200 per square metre.

intro.promise: By the end you’ll be able to list a programme, size a room from its furniture, and compute the gross area and cost from the net.
intro.whyItMatters: The floor area you pay for is measured over the whole building, so it is not the same number as the area of the rooms.

recap.keyIdea: A programme lists the spaces a building must hold, sized from furniture plus clearance and related by adjacency. Gross area is the net area divided by the efficiency, so at 85 percent 68 m² of rooms needs 80 m² of floor.

blocks.text: Cost per square metre applies to the gross area, so a plan with long corridors, which lowers the efficiency, costs more for the same rooms.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson shows how a plan, a section and an elevation record that building at a scale you can measure.

lessons.title: Plan, section and elevation

lead.text: Each view is an **orthographic projection**: the parts of the building are projected straight onto the page along parallel lines, so a length parallel to the page is drawn at its true size and not foreshortened as it would be in a photograph.
The **plan**, the **section** and the **elevation** are drawn with the same scale and the same positions for each feature, so a window that appears in all three can be followed from one to the next.

afterFigure.text: The important point to carry is that they are not three pictures of the outside but three different ways of cutting or looking at the same object.

The plan is cut 1.2 metres above the floor and shows the window as a gap in the wall. The elevation shows the outside face of the south wall with the window. The section cuts through the window and shows the heights. The second view colours the window in all three.

reveal.text: A plan is a *cut*, not a view from above. The next screen shows where the cut goes.

lead.text: Imagine slicing a house horizontally at about **1.2 m above the floor** and lifting off the top. What is left, seen from above, is the **plan**: the walls are cut and drawn solid, and the window appears as an opening in the wall, because the cut passes between its sill at 0.9 m and its head at 2.1 m. The height 1.2 m is chosen for exactly this reason, so that the plan passes through windows and shows doors in their frames.

A **section** is the vertical equivalent. A cutting line is marked across the plan, labelled A at each end, and the building is sliced along it and seen from the side in the direction of the arrow. It is the drawing that shows heights: the thickness of the floor, the build-up of the roof, the depth of the foundation and the head height of a window all appear in it, and they appear nowhere else.

afterFigure.text: What is cut is drawn heavy and often filled solid, and what lies beyond the cut is drawn lighter. A *roof* plan is the one plan that really is a view from above, because nothing has been cut away from it.

lead.text: An **elevation** is a view of an outside face drawn as though you stood far enough away for all its lines to run parallel. It shows the openings, the materials and the profile of the roof, but nothing of the inside, because nothing is cut.

To be measured, a drawing needs a **scale**. A scale of 1:50 means that 1 unit on paper stands for 50 of the same unit in the building, so the 4.2 m width of the room is 4200 mm in the building and 4200 ÷ 50 = 84 mm on the sheet. The first number is the drawing and the second is the building, so a *larger* second number gives a *smaller* drawing.

afterFigure.text: Going from the building to the paper divides by the second number, and going from the paper to the building multiplies by it.

diagram.alt: A bar for the width of a 4.2 metre room at three scales. At 1:20 it is 210 millimetres, at 1:50 it is 84 millimetres and at 1:100 it is 42 millimetres. The bar gets shorter as the second number grows.

reveal.text: Elevations show what a passer-by sees, so that is where materials and window shapes are decided.

steps.headline: Find the length on paper of a wall 6.5 m long at 1:100.

workedSteps.text: A scale compares lengths in the same unit, so convert the wall length to millimetres first.
At 1:100 each millimetre of paper stands for 100 mm of building, so the paper length is the building length divided by 100.
Check the direction: a drawing of a building is smaller than the building, so the answer should be smaller than 6500.
At 1:50 the same wall would be twice as long on paper, because the second number is half as large.

steps.headline: On a 1:20 detail drawing a wall measures 120 mm. Find its length in the building.

workedSteps.text: The scale is 1:20, so 1 mm on paper is 20 mm in the building.
Finding a real length from a paper length runs the other way from the wall in the last example.
Converting the answer to metres shows whether it is a plausible wall height.

lead.text: A section is the drawing that gives heights.

reveal.text: This is how a builder reads a ceiling height from a drawing: a scale rule on the section, or the arithmetic you just did.

lead.text: The scale on a site plan is much smaller than on a room plan.

reveal.text: At 1:200 a 1.2 m window is 6 mm wide, and a 7.6 m garden is 38 mm. A whole plot fits on one sheet, but a window can only be a mark, so the detail belongs on the 1:100 plans.

blocks.text: A room 4.2 m wide, 3.6 m deep and 2.4 m high has a window 1.2 m wide in its south wall, with its sill at 0.9 m and its head at 2.1 m. Each of those numbers can be read from a drawing, but not from the same one: the width of the window shows in the plan, the sill and head heights in the section, and the shape of the opening in the elevation.

Those three kinds of drawing, the **plan**, the **section** and the **elevation**, are how a building is recorded before it exists, and each is drawn to a stated scale, such as 1:50, so that any length on the paper can be measured and multiplied back to its size in the building.

The section cuts through the window and shows the heights. The second view colours the window in all three.

intro.promise: By the end you’ll be able to say what plan, section and elevation each show, and convert any length with a scale such as 1:50.
intro.whyItMatters: A drawing can only be measured if you know which view it is and what its scale is.

recap.keyIdea: A plan is a horizontal cut about 1.2 m above the floor, a section is a vertical cut that shows heights and build-ups, and an elevation is an outside face with no cut. Each is an orthographic projection, so lengths in them can be measured.

blocks.text: A scale of 1:50 means 1 unit on paper stands for 50 in the building: multiply paper lengths by 50 to get real lengths, and divide real lengths by 50 to draw them.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson uses a section to find the dimensions of a stair, starting from the storey height.

lessons.title: Moving through a building

lead.text: Halls, landings, corridors and stairs are the **circulation** of a building. They carry no furniture and no one lives in them, but every room is reached through them, so they count in the gross area that 'From brief to programme' priced, and they decide how the plan can be cut up. In a small house the circulation might take a tenth of the floor, and on a tight plan the stair alone takes about 4.4 m by 0.9 m.

A bathroom, for instance, needs a clear circle about 1.5 m across where a wheelchair can turn, and a door that swings into that circle makes the room unusable however large it is on paper. The figure shows the same 2.4 m bathroom with the door hung two ways.

afterFigure.text: Approved Document M (England) is the source for access guidance of this kind, and national codes differ in the dimensions they use, so these are examples to reason with and not figures to design from.

diagram.alt: A plan of a 2.4 by 2.4 metre bathroom with a 0.9 metre door in the south wall and a 1.5 metre turning circle in the middle. When the door swings in, its arc crosses the circle. When it swings out, the circle is clear.

reveal.text: The height between the floors. The length of the stair is a result, as the next screen shows.

lead.text: Each step of a stair has a **riser**, the vertical rise, and a **going**, the horizontal depth of the tread. Because the stair joins two floors, the sum of its risers must equal the **floor-to-floor height**, and every riser must be the same, so the first move is to choose a whole number of risers n that gives R = H ÷ n close to 175 mm. For H = 2700 mm, n = 16 gives R = 168.75 mm.

The going is then found from a comfort rule, usually credited to the 17th-century French architect François Blondel: **2R + G should be about 630 mm**. Approved Document K for England (2013 edition) states that 2R + G for a private stair should be between 550 and 700 mm. With R = 168.75, G = 630 − 337.5 = 292.5 mm. A flight of 16 risers has 15 goings, because the top riser lands on the floor above, so the run is 15 × 292.5 = 4387.5 mm.

afterFigure.text: Fewer risers mean taller steps with shorter goings and a shorter stair, and more risers give gentler steps and a longer one, so the choice trades comfort against floor area.

diagram.alt: A stair section from a lower floor to a floor 2700 millimetres above, with the riser and going marked. With 15 risers the riser is 180 mm, the going 270 mm and the run 3780 mm. With 16 risers the riser is 168.75, the going 292.5 and the run 4387.5. With 17 risers the riser is 158.82, the going 312.35 and the run 4997.6.

steps.headline: Size a stair for a floor-to-floor height of 2700 mm using 16 risers.

workedSteps.text: The risers must be equal and add up to the storey height.
Use the comfort rule to find the going.
There is one going fewer than risers, so the run of 15 goings is
Check against the example limits: the riser is under 220, the going is over 220 and the pitch is arctan(168.75 ÷ 292.5).

steps.headline: Find the going and the run for a stair with 175 mm risers and 15 goings.

workedSteps.text: Use the comfort rule with the riser given.
That leaves one unknown, the going G.
The stair has 15 goings, so the run is the going multiplied by 15.

reveal.text: The number of risers is chosen so that R comes close to 175 mm; 15 does that for 2600.
A stair of 15 risers is about 4 m long. The next screen compares that with ramps, which are far longer for the same rise.

lead.text: A gradient of 1:12 means a rise of 1 for every 12 along, so a ramp for a rise of 0.6 m is 0.6 × 12 = 7.2 m long, compared with the 4.4 m of a stair that rises 2.7 m. Codes usually ask for gentler slopes than 1:12 on routes meant for wheelchair users, and Approved Document M for England treats about 1:20 as the gradient below which a route is not a ramp at all, so the length in a real design is often longer still.

Approved Document K gives 2.0 m of headroom over a stair, measured vertically from the pitch line, and a stair that climbs into a sloping roof can fail it near the top even if every riser is correct. A steep stair is a *falling* hazard, not only an uncomfortable one, which is why the codes limit the pitch to 42 degrees as well as the sum 2R + G.

afterFigure.text: These dimensions are examples from England’s Approved Documents K and M. Other countries use different limits, and a design must always be checked against the code that applies where the building stands.

reveal.text: At 1:12 the 450 mm rise needs 5.4 m, which is over the 5 m allowed for one flight, and at 1:15 it needs 6.75 m. Either way a ramp is far longer than the stair that climbs the same height, so a ramped entrance is planned with the landscape from the start.
Passing 2R + G is necessary but not sufficient; the pitch limit of 42 degrees and the minimum going of 220 mm are separate checks.

lessons.orientation: Size a stair from the storey height, and check width, headroom and ramp length.

blocks.text: A storey 2700 mm high, measured from one floor to the next, can be climbed in sixteen equal steps of 168.75 mm, and if each tread is then 292.5 mm deep the flight runs 4387.5 mm across the floor. Choose fifteen steps or seventeen instead and the depth of the treads and the length of the flight both change with it, so the numbers of a stair cannot be chosen one at a time.
What ties them together is a comfort rule that twice the height of a step plus its depth should come to about 630 mm.

intro.promise: By the end you’ll be able to size a stair from its floor-to-floor height, and check it against ramp and access limits that your code sets.
intro.whyItMatters: A stair that is cheap to fix on paper is expensive to fix in concrete, and the arithmetic is short.

recap.keyIdea: A stair is sized from the floor-to-floor height: divide it into equal risers near 175 mm, find the going from 2R + G = 630 mm, and take the run as one fewer going than risers. For 2700 mm that is 16 risers of 168.75 mm and a run of 4387.5 mm.

blocks.text: The codes add their own limits, such as the pitch and headroom in England’s Approved Document K and the gradients in Approved Document M, and a 1:12 ramp needs 12 times its rise in length.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns from how people move through a building to how it is held up, by following a load to the ground.

lessons.title: Holding a small building up

reveal.text: A lintel does. The next screen follows the whole route a load takes, with the lintel as one link.

lead.text: The weight of the roof goes into the walls, the weight of the floor goes into its joists and from them into the walls, the walls bear on foundations, and the foundations spread the load over enough soil to hold it. Taken together this is the **load path**, and it must be continuous: a load that arrives at a point with nothing beneath it will bend or break whatever is there.

A window or door opening breaks the wall below it, so something has to bridge the gap. That piece is a **lintel**, a beam that spans the opening and passes the weight above it round the gap to the wall on each side.

afterFigure.text: Walls therefore hold up more than the roof, and an opening is not free: it moves load to the sides, which is why walls beside openings and the ends of lintels need to be solid.

diagram.alt: Three views of how a load reaches the ground. In a section through a two-storey house, roof load runs down the walls to foundations. In the second view, floor load goes through the joists into the walls and down. In an elevation of a wall with a window opening, a lintel above the opening carries the wall's weight to the wall on each side.

lead.text: The **dead load** is the weight of the floor itself and its finishes, here 0.5 kN/m², and the **imposed load** is what people and furniture add, 1.5 kN/m², a value typical for the floors of a house. The two are combined with factors that allow for the chance of the real load being higher than expected: 1.35 on the dead load and 1.5 on the imposed load, the partial factors of the Eurocode basis of design.

The design load is therefore 1.35 × 0.5 + 1.5 × 1.5 = 0.675 + 2.25 = **2.925 kN/m²**, a load per square metre of floor. A joist is a line, so the load must be turned into a load per metre of joist: each joist carries a strip of floor as wide as the spacing between joists, and at 0.4 m the line load is 2.925 × 0.4 = **1.17 kN/m**. Mixing kN/m² with kN/m is the commonest slip in this calculation.

steps.headline: Find the design load and the line load for a floor with dead load 0.5 kN/m² and imposed load 1.5 kN/m², with joists at 0.4 m.

workedSteps.text: The dead and imposed loads are factored separately.
The imposed load has the larger factor.
Add them for the design load on each square metre.
Each joist carries a strip 0.4 m wide, so multiply by the spacing.

reveal.text: Wider spacing loads each joist more, which is why joists at 0.6 m need to be deeper than joists at 0.4 m for the same span.

lead.text: A joist resting on a support at each end sags between them. The sagging is resisted by the **bending moment** in the joist, which is largest at midspan and zero at the supports. For a simply supported span L carrying an even line load w, the largest moment is **M = wL² ÷ 8**. For 1.17 kN/m on a 3.6 m span, M = 1.17 × 3.6² ÷ 8 = 1.17 × 12.96 ÷ 8 = 1.895 kN m.

The span is squared, so a small change in span has a large effect: a joist that is 20 percent longer has a moment 44 percent larger. That is why designers add a beam or wall to shorten spans before they enlarge joists.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows the loading, with each support carrying half of the total load of 4.21 kN, and then the moment diagram, a parabola that peaks in the middle.

The second view adds the bending moment diagram, a parabola that peaks at 1.895 kilonewton metres at midspan and is zero at the supports.

steps.headline: A joist spans 3.0 m and carries 1.17 kN/m. Find the midspan moment.

workedSteps.text: The moment of an evenly loaded simple span is wL² ÷ 8.
The load is 1.17 kN/m and the span is 3.0 m.
The 3.6 m span in the explanation above gave 1.90 kN m, so a shorter span should give a clearly smaller moment.

lead.text: A bending moment is resisted by the stress in the timber, and how well a cross-section resists it is measured by its **section modulus**, Z = b d² ÷ 6 for a rectangle b wide and d deep. The joist must satisfy **Z ≥ M ÷ strength**. With M = 1.895 kN m = 1.895 × 10⁶ N mm and an illustrative design bending strength of 7 N/mm², Z must be at least 270 800 mm³, or about 271 cm³.

A 47 × 195 mm joist has Z = 47 × 195² ÷ 6 = 297 863 mm³ = 297.9 cm³, which exceeds 271 and passes. The 7 N/mm² is only illustrative, since real design strengths depend on the timber grade, how long the load lasts and other factors, and a real joist is also checked for deflection and vibration, which often govern the depth of a floor.

afterFigure.text: Because d is squared, doubling the depth makes the joist four times stronger in bending, while doubling the width only doubles it.

reveal.text: Z grows with the square of the depth but only in step with the width, so adding depth buys more resistance for the same extra timber. That is why floor joists are deep and narrow.
This joist fails at 3.6 m, which is why the example used 195 mm.

lessons.orientation: Trace a load path, convert a floor load to a joist load, and check a timber joist for bending.

blocks.text: A floor in a house carries its own weight and the people and furniture on it, and every newton of that load has to reach the ground through a chain of parts, from the boards to the joists, from the joists to the walls and from the walls to the foundations.

For a timber floor joist, whether its part of the route is strong enough can be checked with three lines of arithmetic: turn the floor load into a load per metre of joist, find the bending moment that load produces at midspan, and compare it with what the joist's cross-section can resist.

recap.keyIdea: A load path is the unbroken route from roof and floors through walls and foundations to the ground, and a lintel keeps it unbroken over an opening. A floor’s design load, 1.35 × dead + 1.5 × imposed, becomes a joist’s line load once it is multiplied by the joist spacing.

blocks.text: The midspan moment is wL² ÷ 8, and the joist passes if its section modulus bd²/6 is at least the moment divided by the design strength. Depth matters because it is squared.

lessons.title: Light

lead.text: The unit of illuminance is the **lux**, which measures the light falling on a surface. A meter reads 10 000 lux outdoors under an overcast sky, and the same meter reads 150 lux at a desk in a room.

Written as a percentage, the share that reaches the desk is the **daylight factor**: DF = indoor illuminance ÷ outdoor illuminance × 100. For these readings DF = 150 ÷ 10 000 × 100 = **1.5 percent**. The measurement is taken under an overcast sky, which is nearly uniform, so the value does not depend on the hour or on which way the window faces, and it does not measure sun at all.

afterFigure.text: Daylight factor falls quickly with distance, so one value for a whole room hides large differences between the window end and the back.

diagram.alt: A section of a room with a window on the left and three desk-height light readings under an overcast sky of 10 000 lux outdoors: 720 lux at 1 metre from the window, 260 lux at 2.5 metres and 120 lux at 4.5 metres. Each is divided by 10 000 to give the daylight factor: 7.2, 2.6 and 1.2 percent.
diagram.caption: Daylight factor at three points in one room. The same sky gives very different values at different distances from the window.

steps.headline: Find the daylight factor for 150 lux indoors and 10 000 lux outdoors.

workedSteps.text: Both readings are illuminances in lux, so their ratio has no unit.
Substitute the readings, with the indoor reading on top.
Multiply by 100 to give a percentage.
A value near 2 percent is often quoted as the level at which a room looks daylit, so 1.5 percent is a little dim.

reveal.text: A factor of 2 percent is the figure often quoted as the average for a room that looks daylit, and 5 percent as one that looks bright.
The window head. The next screen shows the rule that puts a number on it.

lead.text: Daylight from one wall reaches only so far, and a rule of thumb of the form used in BRE guidance (BR 209) puts a limit on it. For a room of depth L from window wall to rear wall, width W and a window head at height Hw above the floor, the room is adequately lit near the back if **L/W + L/Hw ≤ 2/(1 − R)**, where R is the average **reflectance** of the room’s surfaces, a number from 0 for black to 1 for white. With R = 0.5 the limit is 2 ÷ 0.5 = 4.

Take a room 5 m deep and 4 m wide. With the window head at 2.2 m, L/W = 1.25 and L/Hw = 2.27, so the sum is 3.52, which is under 4 and passes. Lower the head to 1.8 m and L/Hw = 2.78, so the sum is 4.03, just over the limit, and the room fails. A deeper room, a narrower one or a lower head all raise the sum.

diagram.alt: A section of a room 5 metres deep with a window in one wall. With the window head at 2.2 metres the depth sum 5/4 + 5/2.2 is 3.52, under the limit of 4, so the room passes. With the head at 1.8 metres the sum is 4.03, over the limit, so it fails. A dashed line from the rear floor to the top of the glass is steeper for the higher window.
diagram.caption: The same room with two window heights. The dashed line is the sky view from the rear of the floor. Use the buttons to lower the window head.

steps.headline: Test a room 6 m deep and 4.5 m wide with the window head at 2.1 m and average reflectance 0.5.

workedSteps.text: The limit for R = 0.5 is 2 ÷ (1 − R).
The room’s own sum is L/W + L/Hw, with L = 6 m, W = 4.5 m and Hw = 2.1 m.
The room is adequately lit near its back wall only when the sum is no larger than the limit, and a larger sum fails the rule.

lead.text: In a room painted pale, light bounces further, so R rises and the limit rises with it: at R = 0.6 the limit is 2 ÷ 0.4 = 5, so the 1.8 m head with a sum of 4.03 would now pass. A dark floor and dark walls lower R and make the same room dim.

When daylight runs out, artificial light fills in, and a point source follows an inverse-square law: illuminance E = I ÷ d², with I in candela and d in metres. A lamp of 400 candela gives 100 lux at 2 m and 25 lux at 4 m, so the lamp should be close to the work.

reveal.text: Halving the distance gives four times the light, because illuminance falls with the square of the distance. Bringing a task close to a lamp or a window helps far more than raising the level of light across the whole room.

lead.text: Painting a room in paler colours raises its average reflectance.

reveal.text: Reflectance changes the limit and leaves the sum alone. Paler surfaces raise the limit, darker ones lower it, and the room's shape and window head are the same either way.

blocks.text: On an overcast day a light meter might read 10 000 lux outdoors and only 150 lux on a desk in a room, so the room is receiving 1.5 percent of the light outside, which is a little dim.

Both the overall level and the fall towards the back depend on the shape of the room and its window rather than on the weather, which is why they can be predicted from the drawings before the room is built. The **daylight factor** gives the first as a single percentage, and a rule comparing the depth of the room with its width and its window tells you whether the back will be adequately lit.

intro.whyItMatters: The shape of a room and its window, both fixed on the drawings, settle whether the back of the room is lit.

recap.keyIdea: The daylight factor is the indoor illuminance as a percentage of the outdoor illuminance under an overcast sky, so 150 lux against 10 000 lux gives 1.5 percent. It describes the room, not the day, and it does not measure sun.

blocks.text: A side-lit room passes the depth rule when L/W + L/Hw is at most 2/(1 − R), so a higher window head, a paler interior or a shallower room each help the back to be lit.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson moves from light to heat, and computes how much heat a wall loses from its layers.

lessons.title: Heat through a wall

reveal.text: The ratio of the conductivities is 35, and the next screen shows why that ratio is the answer.

lead.text: Heat flows from the warm side of a wall to the cold side, and the rate is proportional to the temperature difference. How easily a material lets it through is its **conductivity**, written k and measured in W/mK, which is 0.77 for brick, 0.022 for PIR (rigid polyisocyanurate foam), 0.11 for aircrete block and 0.57 for plaster. A layer of thickness d metres then has a **thermal resistance** R = d ÷ k, in m²K/W.

A wall is several layers in a row, and the same heat passes through each in turn, so their resistances add. Each face of the wall also has a thin film of still air that resists heat flow: a standard value is **0.13** on the inside and **0.04** on the outside. For the wall in the figure, brick gives 0.102 ÷ 0.77 = 0.132, PIR 0.100 ÷ 0.022 = 4.545, block 0.100 ÷ 0.11 = 0.909, plaster 0.013 ÷ 0.57 = 0.023, and the two films give 0.17, a total of **5.78 m²K/W**.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows the layers, the resistances as bars, and the temperature falling through the wall: almost all of the drop happens across the PIR, which is where the resistance is.

diagram.alt: A wall, from inside to outside: 13 mm plaster, 100 mm blockwork, 100 mm PIR insulation and 102 mm brick. The second view shows each layer's thermal resistance, the PIR being 4.55 of the total 5.78. The third view plots temperature from 20 degrees inside to 0 outside, with most of the drop across the insulation.

reveal.text: Wool needs about 60 percent more thickness than PIR for the same resistance, because its conductivity is about 60 percent higher. That is why PIR is chosen where space is tight.

lead.text: The **U-value** says how many watts pass through each square metre of a wall for each degree of temperature difference across it, so its unit is W/m²K. It is the reciprocal of the total resistance: **U = 1 ÷ (Rsi + ΣR + Rse)**. For the wall above, U = 1 ÷ 5.78 = 0.173 W/m²K. Because resistances add and U-values do not, the sum comes first and the reciprocal after.

The heat lost is then **Q = U × A × ΔT**. For 40 m² of this wall with air at 20 °C inside and 0 °C outside, ΔT = 20 K and Q = 0.173 × 40 × 20 = 138 W. Take the PIR out and almost all of the resistance goes with it, so the U-value, and with it the heat lost, rises several times over.

afterFigure.text: For comparison, Approved Document L (England, 2021 edition) gives a limiting U-value of 0.26 W/m²K for the walls of a new dwelling (a notional reference wall is set at 0.18), and Passive House buildings commonly have walls well below that.

steps.headline: Find the U-value of the wall: 102 mm brick, 100 mm PIR, 100 mm block and 13 mm plaster, with the standard surface resistances.

workedSteps.text: Find each layer’s resistance as thickness in metres divided by conductivity.
Brick, PIR, block and plaster in turn.
Add the two surface films, 0.13 inside and 0.04 outside, and the layers together.
U is the reciprocal of the total.

steps.headline: Find the U-value of the same wall with the insulation left out.

workedSteps.text: Remove the PIR’s 4.545 from the total of 5.78.
The U-value of the wall follows from its total resistance, in the same way as before.
Comparing it with the insulated wall’s 0.173 shows how many times more heat the wall loses without the insulation.

reveal.text: A change in outdoor temperature changes the loss in proportion to the new temperature difference, so halving it halves the heat lost.

The PIR wall (0.173) beats the notional 0.18, and the wool wall (0.244) is under the 0.26 limit but not under 0.18, so it costs the design something elsewhere. These figures are for England, and other countries set their own.

lessons.orientation: Compute the U-value of a layered wall from its resistances, and the heat it loses.

blocks.text: A wall of 102 mm of brick, 100 mm of PIR insulation, 100 mm of blockwork and 13 mm of plaster has a **U-value** of 0.173 W/m²K, which means that each square metre of it lets through 0.173 watts for every degree of difference between its two sides. Forty square metres of that wall, between a room at 20 °C and air at 0 °C, lose 138 W, while the same wall with the insulation left out loses about 4.7 times as much.

intro.promise: By the end you’ll be able to compute a wall’s U-value from its layers and use it to find the heat the wall loses.
intro.whyItMatters: The U-value sets how much heat a building loses through its envelope, and so how big its heating system must be.

recap.keyIdea: A layer’s resistance is its thickness divided by its conductivity, resistances in series add, and the U-value is the reciprocal of their sum with the surface films of 0.13 and 0.04. For the example wall U = 1 ÷ 5.78 = 0.173 W/m²K.

blocks.text: The heat lost is U × A × ΔT, so 40 m² at 20 K loses 138 W, and removing the insulation multiplies that by about 4.7.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson counts the heat that leaves through gaps rather than through the wall, and asks when a cold surface will run with water.

lessons.title: Air leakage, condensation and thermal bridges

lead.text: Walls are not the only way heat leaves a building. Air does too: every time warm air leaves through a gap and cold air comes in, the incoming air has to be heated. If the whole volume of the house is replaced n times in an hour, the loss is **H = 0.33 × n × V** in W/K, where V is the volume in m³. The 0.33 is the heat needed per hour to warm 1 m³ of air by 1 K, in watt-hours, because air has a density of about 1.2 kg/m³ and a specific heat of about 1005 J/kgK.

For a house of 150 m³ at 0.5 air changes an hour, H = 0.33 × 0.5 × 150 = **24.75 W/K**, and with 20 K between inside and outside that is 495 W, around the clock. For comparison, 40 m² of the well-insulated wall in the last lesson lost 138 W. The rate **n** is measured in air changes per hour, and for a leaky house it can be four times the figure used here.

diagram.alt: A box for a house of 150 cubic metres with arrows for cold air entering and warm air leaving. At 0.5 air changes per hour the heat loss is 24.75 watts per kelvin, at 1 it is 49.5 and at 2 it is 99.

The answer is 12 °C. The next screen explains where it comes from.

lead.text: Warm air can hold much more water vapour than cold air. If a given parcel of air is cooled without losing any vapour, its **relative humidity** rises until it reaches 100 percent, and the temperature at which that happens is the **dew point**. Air at 20 °C and 60 percent relative humidity has a dew point of 12.0 °C, and at 65 percent it is 13.2 °C. Any surface colder than the dew point cools the air touching it to saturation and collects water, which is **condensation**.

So the test for condensation is a comparison of two temperatures: the temperature of the inside *surface* against the dew point of the room air. The surface temperature is found from the U-value: **Ts = Ti − U × Rsi × ΔT**, where Rsi = 0.13 is the inside surface resistance. For the wall of the last lesson, U = 0.173, so Ts = 20 − 0.173 × 0.13 × 20 = 19.55 °C. For old double glazing with U = 2.8, Ts = 20 − 2.8 × 0.13 × 20 = 12.72 °C.

afterFigure.text: In the graph, the curve is the dew point and the dashed lines are the two surfaces. The window’s line crosses the curve at 62.9 percent humidity, so above that the glass runs with water, while the wall is dry up to 97 percent.

steps.headline: Will the inside surface of old double glazing (U = 2.8 W/m²K) condense when the room is 20 °C at 65 percent humidity and it is 0 °C outside?

workedSteps.text: The temperature drop across the inside film is U × Rsi × ΔT.
Subtract it from the room temperature to get the surface temperature.
The dew point of 20 °C air at 65 percent humidity is 13.2 °C.
The surface is colder than the dew point, so water forms.

steps.headline: Find the surface temperature of the lintel in a wall, where concrete bridges the insulation and the local U-value is 1.2 W/m²K (an illustrative value).

workedSteps.text: The drop across the inside film is U × Rsi × ΔT.
The surface is that much colder than the room air.
The plain wall around the lintel is at 19.55 °C, so the lintel is the colder spot, which is how a bridge shows as a damp stripe.

lead.text: A **thermal bridge** is a place where a more conductive material crosses the insulation, such as a concrete lintel, the edge of a floor slab or a corner. Heat flows through it more easily than through the wall around it, so its inside surface is colder, and it is the first place on a wall where the surface can drop below the dew point and run with water or grow mould. The remedy is detailing, which keeps the insulation continuous around such spots, and not more insulation elsewhere.

Sealing the building cuts the ventilation loss, but people breathe, cook and wash, and the moisture and pollutants they make have to leave somewhere. The usual answer is to make the building airtight and then ventilate it deliberately, often with a system that recovers heat from the outgoing air.

reveal.text: A surface above the dew point stays dry whatever the humidity of the room, so the warm inside face of an insulated wall can stay dry while the cold glass beside it runs with water.
At 65 percent humidity the lintel's 16.88 °C is above the 13.2 °C dew point and stays dry, but in more humid air, from about 82 percent, it is the first surface in the wall to condense.

blocks.text: A house of 150 m³ whose air is replaced half a time each hour loses 24.75 W for every degree between inside and outside, because cold air comes in through gaps, is warmed, and leaves again carrying that heat with it. With 20 degrees between inside and outside that is 495 W, about three and a half times what 40 m² of well-insulated wall loses, and none of it passes through the wall at all.

The same house has a second problem that insulation alone does not fix. Water can run down an old window at 65 percent humidity while the wall beside it stays dry, because the glass is colder than the air's **dew point**, the temperature at which the air can hold no more water vapour, and the wall is not.

recap.keyIdea: Ventilation heat loss is 0.33 × n × V in W/K, so 150 m³ at 0.5 air changes an hour loses 24.75 W/K. Water condenses on any surface colder than the dew point of the room air, and the surface temperature is Ti minus U × Rsi × ΔT.

blocks.text: The old window at 12.72 °C is below the 13.2 °C dew point at 65 percent humidity, so it runs with water, while the insulated wall at 19.55 °C stays dry. Thermal bridges are cold spots, and an airtight building needs ventilation designed in.

lessons.title: Comfort and passive design

steps.headline: A person as a heat source

lead.text: Food is burned in the body at a rate that depends on activity, measured in **met**. One met is 58.2 W per square metre of skin, and an adult has about 1.8 m², so at rest a person gives off about 58.2 × 1.8 = 105 W, roughly a bright lamp. The body must lose that heat at about the rate it is made, or its temperature changes, and comfort is the feeling of losing it at the right rate.

Heat leaves in three ways. **Radiation** goes to every surface in view that is cooler than the skin, **convection** goes to the air moving over the body, and **evaporation** takes heat with moisture from the skin and breath. The figure shows a person between two walls, and the second view cools one of them.

afterFigure.text: The surfaces count as much as the air.

diagram.alt: A person in a room between two walls. Dashed arrows carry heat by radiation to each wall, an arrow rises for convection to the air, and a label notes evaporation. In the first view both walls are at 20 degrees and the operative temperature is 20. In the second view the left wall is at 16, its radiation arrow is heavier, and the operative temperature is 18.

reveal.text: The felt temperature is called the operative temperature, and for these numbers it is 18 °C.

lead.text: A person is comfortable when six factors line up: the **air temperature**, the **mean radiant temperature** of the surrounding surfaces, the air speed, the humidity, the clothing worn and the activity. Four belong to the room and two to the occupant, so no single thermostat reading decides comfort.

To combine the first two, the **operative temperature** is used. At low air speeds it is close to the average of the air and mean radiant temperatures, so with air at 20 °C and walls at 16 °C it is (20 + 16) ÷ 2 = 18 °C.

afterFigure.text: Better insulation raises the surface temperatures of the walls, which is why it improves comfort and not only the bill.

steps.headline: Find the heat given off by a person doing seated office work at 1.2 met.

workedSteps.text: One met is 58.2 W for each square metre of skin.
The skin area of an adult is about 1.8 m², so the heat at 1 met is
Seated work is 1.2 met, so multiply the heat at 1 met by 1.2.
Twenty such people in an office give off 2.5 kW, a heat gain that cooling must remove.

reveal.text: Twenty seated people give off as much heat as a 2.5 kW heater, so a full room can overheat with the heating off.

lead.text: In winter the aim is to **gain** sun through south glazing, **store** it in a heavy floor or wall, and **retain** it with insulation and airtightness. In summer the aim is to **shade** the glass, **ventilate** at night when the air is cool, and let the same mass absorb the day’s heat.

The overhang from the first lesson does the sorting. At latitude 52 the noon sun is 14.6 degrees high in December and passes beneath a 0.6 m overhang into the room, while in June it is 61.4 degrees high and the overhang shades 1.10 m of the wall. **Thermal mass** neither makes heat nor stops it: it stores heat when the room is warm and releases it when the room is cool, which smooths out the swings.

afterFigure.text: Beyond what the winter sun can use, extra glass adds summer overheating and winter heat loss, so the glass area is set by both seasons.

diagram.alt: A section of a south-facing room with glazing, a 0.6 metre overhang and a heavy floor slab. In winter the low noon sun at 14.6 degrees passes under the overhang, through the glass and onto the floor, which stores the heat. In summer the sun at 61.4 degrees is blocked by the overhang, and the slab is cooled by night ventilation.

lessons.orientation: Name the factors of thermal comfort, compute a person’s heat output, and choose passive strategies.

blocks.text: A room at 21 °C can feel colder than one at 19 °C if the first has a wall at 15 °C. The thermometer measures only the air, while a person in the room is also losing heat by radiation to every surface in view, and a cold wall draws more of that heat than a warm one, so the reading on the thermometer is only part of what decides whether a room is comfortable.
Once comfort is understood as the balance of heat leaving the body, a building can protect it with its form alone.

diagram.alt: A person in a room between two walls. Dashed arrows carry heat by radiation to each wall, an arrow rises for convection to the air, and a label notes evaporation. In the first view both walls are at 20 degrees and the operative temperature is 20. In the second view the left wall is at 16, its radiation arrow is heavier, and the operative temperature is 18.
diagram.caption: A person loses heat three ways. A cold wall draws more radiant heat, so the room feels colder than its air temperature says. Use the buttons to cool the left wall.

intro.promise: By the end you’ll be able to find an operative temperature, compute the heat a person gives off, and choose a passive strategy for winter or summer.
intro.whyItMatters: Comfort sets how much heating and cooling a building needs, so it is worth getting right with the form of the building first.

recap.keyIdea: Comfort needs air and radiant temperature, air speed, humidity, clothing and activity together, and the operative temperature averages the first two: air 20 °C with walls at 16 °C is 18 °C. A person at 1.2 met gives off 1.2 × 58.2 × 1.8 = 126 W.

blocks.text: Passive design gains, stores and retains sun in winter and shades, ventilates and uses mass in summer, and thermal mass only stores and releases heat. A fixed overhang over south glass admits the winter sun and shades the summer sun.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to the roof, which keeps the weather out and sets how rain is shed.

lessons.title: Roofs, rain and damp

lead.text: A **flat roof** is not flat: it is laid to a fall, such as 1:40, towards a gutter or outlet, so that water runs off instead of lying in pools. A **mono-pitch** roof slopes one way, a **gable** roof has two slopes that meet at a ridge, and a **hip** roof slopes on all four sides.

The slope is the **pitch**, measured as an angle from the horizontal. Different coverings need different minimum pitches, and a steeper roof sheds water faster, gives more room beneath it and also costs more in walls and covering.

reveal.text: The ridge is 1.73 m above the eaves, and the next screen shows the triangle that gives it.

lead.text: Cut a gable roof across its span and its section is an isosceles triangle. Split it down the middle and each half is a right triangle whose base is **half the span**, whose height is the **rise** from eaves to ridge, and whose angle at the eaves is the pitch. Since tan(pitch) = rise ÷ half-span, the rise is **half-span × tan(pitch)**.

For a span of 6 m the half-span is 3 m, and at 30 degrees the rise is 3 × tan 30° = 3 × 0.5774 = **1.73 m**. The relation runs backwards too: a rise of 1.0 m over a half-span of 2.5 m gives tan(pitch) = 0.4, so the pitch is arctan 0.4 = **21.8 degrees**.

afterFigure.text: The rise grows faster than the angle does, because the tangent steepens as the angle increases.

diagram.alt: A gable roof on a 6 metre span drawn at three pitches. The ridge rises 1.09 metres above the eaves at 20 degrees, 1.73 metres at 30 degrees and 2.52 metres at 40 degrees. The rise is the half-span of 3 metres times the tangent of the pitch.
diagram.caption: The same building with three roof pitches, at 56 pixels per metre. A steeper pitch raises the ridge. Use the buttons to change the pitch.

steps.headline: Find the ridge height above the eaves for a 6 m span at 30 degrees, and then the pitch of a roof with a 1.0 m rise over a 2.5 m half-span.

workedSteps.text: The roof section splits into two right triangles, each with half the span as its base.
Find the rise from the half-span and the pitch.
To go the other way, divide the rise by the half-span to get the tangent.
The pitch is the angle with that tangent.

steps.headline: A roof rises 1.5 m over a half-span of 3.0 m. Find its pitch.

workedSteps.text: The tangent of the pitch is the rise over the half-span.
The pitch is the angle with that tangent.
Compare the roof with the 30 degree roof of the last example: it rises less over a half-span of the same size, so its pitch should be lower.

reveal.text: The same triangle works for any gable: only the half-span and the pitch change.

lead.text: Rain comes straight down, so the amount a roof catches depends on the area it presents to the sky, which is its **plan area**, not the larger area of its sloping surface. A roof 6 m by 8 m in plan has 48 m² of plan area, and at 30 degrees its sloped surface is 48 ÷ cos 30° = 55.4 m², but both catch the same rain.

One millimetre of rain on one square metre is one litre, so **Q = i × A**, with i in mm/h and A in m², gives litres per hour. For an intensity of 50 mm/h on 40 m², Q = 2000 L/h = 2.0 m³/h, and dividing by 3600 gives **0.56 L/s**. Design rainfall differs from place to place, so the 50 mm/h used here is only an example; gutters and downpipes are sized for the flow that a local code specifies.

reveal.text: Both areas are there to be used, but rain falls straight down, so only the plan area counts and the extra sloping surface catches no more rain.
Divide by 3600 last, so that litres per hour become litres per second.

lead.text: Moisture in the ground can rise through the brickwork by capillary action, and rain striking the ground can splash up the face of the wall. A **damp-proof course** is a waterproof layer laid across the full thickness of the wall to stop the first. For it to stop the second as well, it must sit above the splash, and a guideline from UK practice is at least 150 mm above the adjoining ground.

The course can be defeated from outside: if a path or a flower bed raises the ground until it covers the course, water gets into the wall above the barrier. The remedy is to keep the ground level below the course, or to fall the paving away from the wall.

diagram.alt: A section through the base of a wall with the ground on its left and a damp-proof course set in the brickwork. In the first view the course sits 150 millimetres above the ground, so splashing rain and rising damp stay below it. In the second view the ground has been raised above the course, so water reaches the wall above it.
diagram.caption: The damp-proof course is a barrier that must stay above the ground. Use the buttons to raise the ground.

lead.text: A flat roof is described by a fall instead of an angle.

reveal.text: A fall of 100 mm across 4 m is about 1.4 degrees, a slope too small to see but enough to drain.

blocks.text: A gable roof over a house 8 m long and 6 m wide covers 48 m² in plan, and in a heavy shower of 50 mm an hour it has to carry away 0.67 litres of water every second, all of it gathered into gutters and taken down pipes to the drains.

Water reaches a building from below as well, rising through masonry from wet ground and splashing up from paving, and a wall is protected from it by a **damp-proof course**, a waterproof layer built across the wall above the ground.

intro.promise: By the end you’ll be able to compute a ridge height from a pitch, rain flow from a roof’s plan area, and say where a damp-proof course goes.
intro.whyItMatters: A roof that sheds water badly causes the damp that other lessons try to avoid.

recap.keyIdea: The rise of a gable roof is the half-span times the tangent of the pitch, so a 6 m span at 30 degrees rises 1.73 m, and the reverse step, the inverse tangent, gives the pitch from a rise. Rainwater flow is the rainfall intensity times the plan area, because rain falls vertically.

blocks.text: A damp-proof course stops water rising and, if it is kept above the ground, also stops splash from reaching the wall above it.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson sets out the drawings that carry all these decisions to a builder, and the scale each is drawn at.

lessons.title: How a small building is drawn

lead.text: Drawings are instructions. The client reads them to check the building is the one they asked for, the planning authority reads them to decide whether it may be built, and the builder reads them to build it, and with the contract they define what has been agreed. A small building therefore has a **drawing set**: a site plan, floor plans, sections, elevations and details.

On the site plan at 1:500 the house is a small block 16 mm by 10 mm, enough to show where it stands, while at 1:100 it is 80 by 50 mm and its rooms can be read. At 1:20 only a corner of it fits on the sheet, but the layers of a wall can be drawn.

reveal.text: The drawing is the site plan, and its scale is the smallest of the set because it has the most to fit on one sheet.

lead.text: A **site plan** at 1:500 to 1:200 shows the plot, the building’s footprint, the road, levels and north. **Floor plans, sections and elevations** at 1:100 to 1:50 show the rooms, walls and openings, and a section is drawn with the cut parts heavy and what lies beyond thin. **Details** at 1:20 to 1:5 show how parts join: a wall base, a window sill, the edge of a roof.
A 12 m wall at 1:100 is 12 000 ÷ 100 = **120 mm** on paper, and 100 mm of wall in a detail at 1:5 is 100 ÷ 5 = **20 mm**.

afterFigure.text: A drawing carries its scale in its title block and often as a bar scale as well, so that the scale survives if the sheet is reduced.

reveal.text: A drawing at 1:5 is the largest of the usual scales, and the sill detail on it can show every layer.

lead.text: On a plan the walls cut by the section are drawn **heavy**, and what lies beneath or beyond is drawn **light**, so the eye finds the structure first. A window is a gap in the wall crossed by thin parallel lines, a door has an arc showing how its leaf swings, and a stair has parallel treads with an arrow and the word UP. A **grid** of lettered and numbered lines gives each wall and column a name, and a north arrow says which way the plan faces.

Lengths are given by **dimension strings**, lines with end marks and a number, usually in millimetres and in tiers: the first tier gives each opening and wall, the second the lengths between grid lines, and the last the overall length. In the figure the 5000 and 3000 add up to the 8000 overall, and a reader can check the strings against each other.

afterFigure.text: A drawing that omits a dimension makes the builder scale it off the sheet, which is how mistakes begin.

The second view adds dimension strings: 5000 plus 3000 in a first tier, 8000 overall in a second, and 5000 for the depth.

lead.text: A scale is true only at the paper size the drawing was made for. If a 1:50 drawing made for A1 is printed at 50 percent on A3, every length is halved, so the print is at 1:100 and a 1:50 rule reads half the true length. A bar scale drawn on the sheet shrinks with it and stays correct, and builders are told to use stated dimensions in preference to measuring the print.

The UK’s RIBA Plan of Work, for example, names stages from strategic definition and briefing, through concept and technical design, to construction and handover, and drawings are issued at each, with the early ones showing intent and the last ones giving instructions to build. A drawing is therefore dated and numbered, and only the latest issue is used on site.

steps.headline: A wall measures 30 mm on an A3 print of a 1:50 drawing made on A1. Find its real length.

workedSteps.text: A1 to A3 halves each length, so the print is half the size of the original.
Halving the paper lengths doubles the ratio, so the print is no longer at 1:50.
Multiply the measured length by the new ratio.
A reading with the original 1:50 rule would have been wrong by a factor of two.

reveal.text: At 1:50 the house is 180 × 120 mm on the sheet. The same division, real length over the second number of the scale, gives any line.

blocks.text: A house 8 m long is 16 mm long on a drawing at 1:500 and 80 mm long on one at 1:100, while at 1:20 a single corner of it fills the sheet. No one drawing could serve the client who wants to see the rooms, the authority that checks the plot and the builder who has to fix the window sill, so a small building is described by a **set of drawings**, each at the scale that suits its purpose.
What makes the set readable is convention: heavy lines for what is cut, thin lines for what lies beyond, a symbol for each door and window, a grid and a north arrow, and dimensions that add up.

intro.promise: By the end you’ll be able to name the drawings in a set, match them to their scales, and read the symbols and dimensions of a plan.
intro.whyItMatters: Drawings are the instructions and the contract for a building, so they have to be readable by someone who never met the designer.

recap.keyIdea: A drawing set holds a site plan at 1:500 to 1:200, plans, sections and elevations at 1:100 to 1:50, and details at 1:20 to 1:5, and a length on paper is the real length divided by the scale ratio. Conventions of line weight, symbols, grid, north arrow and dimension strings make a plan readable without questions.

blocks.text: A print is true to scale only at its original size, so a 1:50 drawing printed at 50 percent is at 1:100, and a bar scale on the sheet keeps the reading correct.

recap.nextHook: The last lesson takes all of this together on one small cabin, from the brief to a heat-loss check.

lessons.title: A small building, end to end

lead.text: The brief is a cabin 6 m by 4 m for two people. Its footprint is 6 × 4 = 24 m², which is the gross area, and at the 85 percent efficiency of the second lesson its net area is 24 × 0.85 = **20.4 m²**. A programme that fits is a main room of 12.4 m² for living and sleeping, a bath of 3 m², a kitchen of 3 m² and a store of 2 m², which add up to 20.4 m². At 2200 per m² of gross area, an illustrative rate, the cabin costs 24 × 2200 = 52 800.
A feature that adds area, such as a porch, adds cost at the same rate, so the budget is tested before the features are added.

The plan shows a main room, a bath and a kitchen with 4 square metres of glazing on the south wall, a footprint of 24 square metres and a net area of 20.4. The section shows the floor joists spanning 4 metres and a mono-pitch roof at 10 degrees. The elevation shows the glazing band under an overhang.

reveal.text: Only 85 percent of the 28 m² is usable, but all of it is built and paid for.

lead.text: The first lesson put the long wall to the sun, so the 4 m² of glazing, a band 3.3 m wide and 1.2 m high between sill 0.9 m and head 2.1 m, goes on the south wall. At latitude 52 a 0.6 m overhang shades 1.10 m of the wall in June and 0.16 m in December, so the winter sun reaches the glass and the summer sun does not.

The cabin’s main room is 4 m deep and 6 m wide, and with the window head at 2.1 m the depth rule gives L/W + L/Hw = 4/6 + 4/2.1 = 0.67 + 1.90 = **2.57**, comfortably below the limit of 4. The daylight reaches the north wall, and the same glass admits winter sun that the thermal mass of the floor can store.

reveal.text: Turned the other way, the main room is 6 m deep and 4 m wide, and the sum is 4.36, over the limit. The long wall faces the sun so that the room is shallow and the glazing is long.

lead.text: The floor joists run across the 4 m width at 0.4 m spacing, with the 2.925 kN/m² design load of the fifth lesson, so the line load is 1.17 kN/m. For a 4 m span the moment is M = 1.17 × 4² ÷ 8 = **2.34 kN m**, and with the illustrative design strength of 7 N/mm² the section modulus must be at least 2.34 × 10⁶ ÷ 7 = 334 000 mm³, or **334 cm³**.

The 47 × 195 mm joist that suited a 3.6 m span has Z = 297.9 cm³ and fails here, because the longer span raised the moment by about 23 percent. A 47 × 220 mm joist has Z = 47 × 220² ÷ 6 = 379.1 cm³ and passes.

afterFigure.text: A change in one dimension, the width of the cabin, changed the size of a member, and that member sets the depth of the floor and so the height of the building above the ground.

steps.headline: Check a 47 × 220 mm floor joist over a 4 m span, with joists at 0.4 m, a dead load of 0.5 kN/m² and an imposed load of 1.5 kN/m².

workedSteps.text: The design load per square metre is the factored dead and imposed loads.
Each joist carries a strip 0.4 m wide.
The midspan moment of an even load on a simple span is wL² ÷ 8.
The section modulus the joist needs is the moment over the design strength.
The 220 mm joist has more than that, so it passes.

steps.headline: Find the heat-loss rate of the cabin’s walls and glazing together.

workedSteps.text: The gross wall area is the perimeter times the height.
The glazing is not wall, so its 4 m² comes off.
The walls’ heat-loss rate is their U-value times their net area.
The glazing adds its own heat-loss rate, from its area and its U-value of 1.4 W/m²K, and the walls and glazing together lose the sum of the two.

lead.text: Heat leaves the cabin through five routes, and their rates in W/K add. The walls give 7.6, the glazing 5.6, a roof of 24 m² at an assumed U = 0.12 gives 2.9 and a floor of 24 m² at an assumed U = 0.15 gives 3.6, and ventilation at 0.5 air changes an hour in 57.6 m³ gives 0.33 × 0.5 × 57.6 = **9.5**. The total is **29.2 W/K**, so with 20 K between inside and outside the cabin needs 584 W.

The order matters. A cabin with uninsulated walls would lose 35.6 W/K through them and need 1144 W, almost twice as much, so spending on insulation and airtightness first is the **fabric-first** approach: the fabric is improved before heating is added, and the heating system that is left is small. Two occupants at 126 W each already give 252 W, about 43 percent of the 584 W.

afterFigure.text: The roof and floor U-values are assumed for the example, and the surface-temperature check from the air lesson gives the glazing at 20 − 1.4 × 0.13 × 20 = 16.4 °C, above the 13.2 °C dew point at 65 percent humidity, so it stays dry.

diagram.alt: A bar chart of the cabin's heat loss in watts per kelvin. With insulated walls: walls 7.6, glazing 5.6, roof 2.9, floor 3.6 and ventilation 9.5, a total of 29.2, which is 584 watts at 20 kelvin. With uninsulated walls the wall bar grows to 35.6 and the total to 57.2, which is 1144 watts.

reveal.text: Ventilation, at 9.5 of 26.8 W/K, is now larger than the walls at 7.6. The lesson's answer is to make the cabin airtight and ventilate it deliberately, recovering heat from the outgoing air.

lead.text: Thinning the insulation in the walls would save money when the cabin is built.

reveal.text: The saving on insulation is paid back many times in the cost of a larger heater and its fuel.
Doubling the glazing adds 5.6 W/K, which is 112 W at 20 K, and it also lets in more summer sun, so the overhang and the depth rule are checked again before the change is agreed.

lessons.orientation: Combine site, area, structure, light and heat to check a small cabin design.
lessons.reviewLabel: A small building, end to end
lessons.nextAction: You can now read a site, size a stair and a joist, test light, and compute the heat a small building loses.

blocks.text: A cabin 6 m by 4 m for two people has a footprint of 24 m² and a net area of 20.4 m². Its south wall carries 4 m² of glazing under a 0.6 m overhang, its floor joists span 4 m, and its heat loss comes to 29.2 W/K, which is 584 W when it is 20 °C inside and 0 °C outside.

Each of those numbers depends on the others, since the width sets how far the joists span and so how deep they must be, the glazing sets both how much light reaches the back of the room and how much heat escapes through the glass, and the losses through the walls and the air set the size of the heater.
