intro.promise: By the end you’ll be able to check a small building’s area, light, floor structure and heat loss together, and see how one decision affects the rest.
intro.whyItMatters: A design is a set of linked decisions, and the arithmetic is how you check them.

recap.keyIdea: The cabin’s footprint is 24 m² with a net area of 20.4 m² at 85 percent efficiency, its main room passes the depth rule at 2.57, its floor needs 47 × 220 mm joists for the 4 m span, and its heat loss is 29.2 W/K. Each result is a check of one decision against the brief.

blocks.text: Because the checks are linked, a change in one place has to be followed through the others, and a fabric-first approach improves the walls, roof, floor and airtightness before any heating system is sized.

questions.prompt: On 21 June in southern England, at latitude 52 degrees north, roughly where on the horizon does the sun rise?
hints: Think of the sun path as a circle tilted about the horizon.
Due east is the answer for only two dates in the year.
questions.onCorrect: On 21 June at latitude 52 the sun rises about 50 degrees from north, which is north-east, and sets in the north-west. Due east is reached only at the equinoxes.

misconceptions.feedback: The sun rises due east only at the equinoxes, in March and September. In midsummer its whole path has swung to the north of that.
South of east is where the sun rises in midwinter. In June the path has swung to the other side of east, towards the north-east.

acceptedIdeas: Well north of east
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Well north of east

choices.label: Due east, as it does on every day of the year
Well south of east
Well north of east

questions.prompt: Your plot is at latitude 40 degrees north. A neighbour's blank wall, 6 m high, runs east to west 8 m due south of your south wall. At noon on 21 December the sun altitude is 26.56 degrees. How high up your south wall does the noon sun reach, in metres to one decimal place?
hints: Draw the ray that just grazes the top of the neighbour's wall and follow it on to your wall.
Over the 8 m of ground between the walls the ray drops by 8 × tan(altitude).
The sun reaches your wall at the neighbour's height less that drop.
questions.onCorrect: The sun reaches your wall only above 2.0 m, so a window with its head at 2.1 m catches almost none of it. South glazing here would have to move up, or the living space further north.

misconceptions.feedback: 4.0 m is how far the ray drops across the gap. The height where it lands is what remains of the wall's 6 m.
That is the length of the neighbour's shadow on level ground. Your wall cuts that shadow short, so the question is how high its edge climbs on your wall.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Drop over 8 m = 8 × tan 26.56° = 4.00 m. Height reached = 6 − 4.00 = 2.0 m.

questions.prompt: Why is the noon sun higher in June than in December at the same place?
hints: Think about what changes between June and December: the distance, the sun, or the angle of Earth’s axis?
The sun's distance and its own motion do not follow the seasons. Ask what stays fixed while Earth goes round the sun.
questions.onCorrect: The declination swings between +23.44 and −23.44 degrees because the axis keeps pointing the same way while Earth orbits, and Earth is nearest the sun in early January.

misconceptions.feedback: Earth is closest to the sun in early January, which is midwinter in the north, so distance cannot be what lifts the June sun.
The sun does not travel north and south. What changes is where Earth stands in its orbit, and with it the direction in which the sun is overhead.

acceptedIdeas: Earth’s axis is tilted, so the Northern Hemisphere leans towards the sun in June
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Earth’s axis is tilted, so the Northern Hemisphere leans towards the sun in June

choices.label: Earth’s axis is tilted, so the Northern Hemisphere leans towards the sun in June
The sun itself moves north in the summer, so it crosses the sky higher up each noon
Earth is nearer the sun in June, so the sun looks higher in the sky

questions.prompt: A 0.8 m overhang sits above a south window at latitude 52 degrees north, and the window's sill is 1.1 m below the overhang. At noon on 21 June the sun altitude is 61.4 degrees. How far down the wall does the overhang's shadow reach, in metres to two decimal places?
hints: The ray touches the tip of the overhang and falls steeply on the wall.
The drop on the wall is the overhang depth multiplied by tan(altitude).
Compare your answer with the 1.1 m to the sill when you have it.
questions.onCorrect: The shadow reaches 1.47 m, past the sill at 1.1 m, so the window is shaded at noon in June. In December, at 14.6 degrees, the same overhang shades only 0.21 m, so winter sun still gets in.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by the tangent instead of multiplying. Here the shadow runs down the wall, and its depth is the overhang times tan(altitude).

questions.prompt: A house stands at latitude 35 degrees south. Which of its walls faces the winter sun for most of the day?
hints: At noon the sun stands over a latitude between the two tropics, 23.44 degrees either side of the equator.
From 35 degrees south, in which direction along the meridian do you look to find the equator?
questions.onCorrect: In the Southern Hemisphere the sun at noon is in the north, so the formula uses the distance between latitude and declination: 90 − |−35 − (+23.44)| = 31.6 degrees in the June winter.

misconceptions.feedback: The east wall gets the sun only in the morning, and in winter that sun is low and brief.
That rule belongs to the other hemisphere. Below the equator the sun at noon stands on the equator side of you, and the equator is not in the direction you named.
The west wall gets the sun only in the evening, and in winter that sun is low and brief.

acceptedIdeas: The north wall
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The north wall

choices.label: The east wall
The north wall
The south wall
The west wall

questions.prompt: A house plan from London puts the living room and its large windows on the south wall to collect winter sun. A client in Sydney, at latitude 34 degrees south, asks to build the same plan unchanged. What is the problem?
hints: Ask where the noon sun stands in the sky in the Southern Hemisphere.
The wall that collects winter sun faces the equator.
questions.onCorrect: At 34 degrees south the noon sun is 32.6 degrees up in the north on 21 June, which is midwinter there, so the north wall is the one that collects it. The plan has to be flipped to suit the hemisphere.

misconceptions.feedback: In the Southern Hemisphere the noon sun stands in the north, so a south wall looks away from the sun all year and stays cool and dim in winter.
The sun rises due east only at the equinoxes. East glass catches morning sun, and does not collect the low noon sun that heats a house in winter.

acceptedIdeas: The glass should go on the north wall, because the noon sun stands in the north there
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The glass should go on the north wall, because the noon sun stands in the north there

choices.label: The glass should go on the north wall, because the noon sun stands in the north there
Nothing needs to change, since a south wall collects the winter sun in both hemispheres
The glass should go on the east wall, because the sun always rises due east

questions.prompt: At latitude 52 degrees north you plan a south-facing living room. A 9 m high block stands 12 m due south of your south wall. At noon on 21 December the sun altitude is 14.56 degrees. What does this tell you?
hints: Work out how long the block's shadow is at noon in December and compare it with the 12 m gap.
Then ask how high up your wall the shadow's edge climbs.
questions.onCorrect: The block's shadow is 9 ÷ tan 14.6° = 34.7 m, well past your wall, and the ray that clears the block meets your wall at 5.9 m. The ground floor gets no winter sun, so the living space has to move.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the June altitude. In December the sun is only 14.6 degrees up, and the shadow is far longer.
A block that is 9 m high and 12 m away blocks any ray lower than about 37 degrees, and the December sun is much lower than that.

acceptedIdeas: The shadow reaches about 35 m, so your south wall is shaded up to about 5.9 m
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The shadow reaches about 35 m, so your south wall is shaded up to about 5.9 m

choices.label: The shadow reaches about 35 m, so your south wall is shaded up to about 5.9 m
The block's shadow is about 5 m long, so it falls short of the room
The sun is due south at noon and the block is only 12 m away, so the sun passes over it

questions.prompt: A client’s rooms add up to 68 m². Compared with 68 m², the building’s floor area is likely to be
hints: Where do the walls between rooms stand in the 68 m² total?
Rooms are measured to the inside of their walls. Ask what stands between two rooms.
questions.onCorrect: Walls, corridors and services take roughly 15 percent of the floor in a small house, so 68 m² of rooms needs about 80 m² of floor.

misconceptions.feedback: The rooms are only the inside of the building. Walls, halls and stairs take floor area too.
Rooms do not overlap: each wall is a thickness that belongs to neither room, which adds area.

acceptedIdeas: larger, because walls, halls and services take space too
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: larger, because walls, halls and services take space too

choices.label: larger, because walls, halls and services take space too
about 68 m², since the rooms are the whole of the building
smaller, because neighbouring rooms overlap at their shared walls

questions.prompt: Why is gross area found by dividing the net area by the efficiency?
hints: Write efficiency as a fraction of net and gross.
Efficiency is a part divided by a whole. Ask which of net and gross is the whole.
questions.onCorrect: Efficiency is net ÷ gross, so at 0.85 the rooms are 85 percent of the gross. Multiplying 68 by 0.85 would give a smaller number, which cannot be the larger gross.

misconceptions.feedback: Efficiency is not the added share. It is net ÷ gross, the share of the gross that is usable room.
Dividing by a number below 1 makes the result larger, which is what is needed, since gross is bigger than net.

acceptedIdeas: Efficiency is the net share of the gross, so gross = net ÷ efficiency
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Efficiency is the net share of the gross, so gross = net ÷ efficiency

choices.label: Efficiency is the share added on for walls, so gross = net ÷ efficiency
Dividing by a number below 1 makes the result smaller
Efficiency is the net share of the gross, so gross = net ÷ efficiency

questions.prompt: A client gives you a list of the rooms they want. In what order do you work from that list to a build cost?
hints: Each step needs a number that the step before it produces.
Cost is charged on one of the two areas, and that area is found from the other.
questions.onCorrect: Each step feeds the next: rooms have no area until they are sized, the net area is their sum, and cost is charged on the gross area that net area implies.

items: List the spaces the household needs
Size each room from its furniture and clearances
Add the room areas to get the net area
Divide the net area by the efficiency to get the gross area
Multiply the gross area by the rate per square metre

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: List the spaces first, size each one from its furniture, add them to get the net area, divide by the efficiency to get the gross area, and only then multiply by the rate, because the rate is charged on the gross area.

questions.prompt: Plan A holds 68 m² of rooms at 85 percent efficiency. Plan B has the same rooms, but long corridors bring its efficiency down to 75 percent. At 2200 per m² of gross area, how much more does Plan B cost to build, to the nearest 100?
hints: Find the gross area of each plan from net ÷ efficiency.
The two gross areas differ by the floor that Plan B spends on corridors.
Price only the difference in area, since that is what changes between the plans.
questions.onCorrect: The corridors add 10.7 m² that no one lives in, and that floor is paid for at the full rate, which is why a compact plan is cheaper to build.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Plan A gross = 68 ÷ 0.85 = 80.0 m²; Plan B gross = 68 ÷ 0.75 = 90.7 m². Difference 10.7 m² × 2200 = 23,467, which is 23,500 to the nearest 100.

questions.prompt: An architect prices a small house by multiplying the 68 m² of room areas in the programme by 2200 per m². The builder's price comes back higher. What did the architect overlook?
hints: Think about the floor that is not part of any room.
Which of the two areas does the rate per square metre apply to?
questions.onCorrect: At 85 percent efficiency the gross area is 80 m², so 12 m² of floor goes on the things that hold the rooms together, and it is built and paid for like any other.

misconceptions.feedback: The rate is charged on the floor of the building. The plot area matters to the site plan and has no floor to price.
Multiplying shrinks the area to 57.8 m², when walls and halls should add to it. Efficiency is net ÷ gross, so gross = net ÷ efficiency.

acceptedIdeas: Walls, halls and the stair also take floor, so the rate applies to about 80 m²
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Walls, halls and the stair also take floor, so the rate applies to about 80 m²

choices.label: Walls, halls and the stair also take floor, so the rate applies to about 80 m²
The rate applies to the plot area, so the garden should have been included
Efficiency should have been applied by multiplying 68 by 0.85, which gives 57.8 m²

questions.prompt: A programme lists the rooms of a small house. Which of these count in the net area, and which only in the gross area?
hints: The net area is the floor inside the rooms and nothing else.
Ask whether a person could be said to live in that space.
questions.onCorrect: Net is the floor of the rooms themselves. Everything that holds the rooms together adds to the gross.

items.label: The floor of the living room
items.explanation: It is a room in the programme.

items.label: The floor of a double bedroom
items.explanation: It is a room in the programme.

items.label: The floor of the bathroom
items.explanation: It is a room in the programme.

items.label: The hall that links the rooms
items.explanation: It carries people between rooms and is not one of them.

items.label: The floor taken up by the stair
items.explanation: It joins the floors and is not a room.

items.label: The thickness of the walls between rooms
items.explanation: It separates rooms and lies outside every one of them.

items.label: The boiler cupboard
items.explanation: It holds services and is not a room the household lives in.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The living room, the double bedroom and the bathroom count in the net area. The hall, the stair, the wall thickness and the boiler cupboard are in the gross area only.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a programme for a small house, rather than a design?
hints: The programme comes before the drawing of the building.
A programme says what is needed, and a design says how it is built. Ask which option says only what is needed.
questions.onCorrect: The programme says what must be provided before anyone decides what it looks like.

misconceptions.feedback: An elevation is a design drawing, and it comes after the programme.
Cost is one check on the programme, but it does not say what spaces are needed.
Those are construction choices that follow from the spaces, not a list of them.

acceptedIdeas: A list of the spaces, their areas and how they relate
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A list of the spaces, their areas and how they relate

choices.label: A list of the spaces, their areas and how they relate
A drawing of the front elevation and all its materials
A costing of the walls at so much per square metre
A schedule of the roof pitch and the tile type

questions.prompt: What does a floor plan show?
hints: Could you see the rooms of a house from directly above its roof?
A plan is cut at about 1.2 m. Ask what that lets you see that a view from above would not.
questions.onCorrect: A plan is cut at about 1.2 m so that it passes through the windows, which is why they appear as openings in the walls.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a roof plan. A floor plan cuts through the walls so that the rooms inside can be seen.
A plan shows the rooms, doors and windows as well as the outline. It is cut, so it records what is inside.

acceptedIdeas: A horizontal slice through the walls, seen from above
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A horizontal slice through the walls, seen from above

choices.label: A horizontal slice through the walls, seen from above
Only the outline of the walls where they meet the ground
The whole building seen from directly above, roof included

questions.prompt: What is the name of the drawing that shows one outside face of a building, with no cut?
hints: It is a view, not a cut.
The word is also used for height above a datum.
questions.onCorrect: An elevation shows the face with its openings and materials, but nothing inside, because no cut has been made.

misconceptions.feedback: A section is a cut, which shows the inside. The view asked for is the outside face with no cut.
A plan is a horizontal cut. The view asked for looks straight at a vertical face.

acceptedIdeas: elevation
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: elevation

questions.prompt: On a 1:20 detail a wall measures 120 mm. How long is it in the building, in millimetres?
hints: 1:20 means 1 mm on paper stands for 20 mm in the building.
The building is larger than the drawing.
Multiply the length on paper by the second number of the scale.
questions.onCorrect: Going from paper to building multiplies by the second number, so 120 mm at 1:20 is 2.4 m, a normal ceiling height.

misconceptions.feedback: 6 divides by 20. Real lengths are larger than lengths on paper, so multiply.

questions.prompt: A client wants a 2.4 m tall wardrobe in the main room. On the 1:50 section, the floor to ceiling height measures 52 mm. Will the wardrobe fit?
hints: Which drawing gives heights, and what does a 1:50 scale do to each length?
Convert the 52 mm on the sheet to a length in the building, then compare it with 2.4 m.
questions.onCorrect: 52 mm × 50 = 2600 mm, so the ceiling is 2.6 m and the wardrobe clears it by 200 mm.

misconceptions.feedback: The section is drawn at 1:50. Reading it at 1:100 doubles the height.
Heights are exactly what a section shows. An elevation shows the outside face and cannot give floor to ceiling height.

acceptedIdeas: Yes, 52 mm at 1:50 is 2.6 m, which leaves 200 mm above it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes, 52 mm at 1:50 is 2.6 m, which leaves 200 mm above it

choices.label: Yes, 52 mm at 1:50 is 2.6 m, which leaves 200 mm above it
Yes, 52 mm at 1:100 is 5.2 m, which leaves plenty of room
It cannot be told, because only an elevation shows heights

questions.prompt: A 1:200 site plan shows a whole 38 m wide plot on one sheet. A colleague suggests drawing every window on it at its true width, which is 1.2 m for each. How wide is a window on the paper, and what does that tell you?
hints: Divide the real width by the second number of the scale, in the same unit.
Ask whether a mark that wide could show an opening and a frame.
questions.onCorrect: At 1:200 a 1.2 m window is 6 mm wide, and a 7.6 m garden is 38 mm, so the sheet is good for position and boundaries and not for openings.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by 200. A larger second number makes the drawing smaller, so the width on paper is the real width divided by 200.
That divides by 2000. 1200 mm ÷ 200 is 6 mm.

acceptedIdeas: 6 mm, too small to read, so windows are left to the 1:100 plans
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 6 mm, too small to read, so windows are left to the 1:100 plans

choices.label: 240 mm, so every window would crowd out its neighbours on the sheet
6 mm, too small to read, so windows are left to the 1:100 plans
0.6 mm, a line so fine that it would not print on the sheet

questions.prompt: A bathroom has a small window with its sill 1.6 m above the floor. The floor plan is cut about 1.2 m above the floor. How does that window appear on the plan?
hints: Picture the slice at 1.2 m and ask whether it passes through the window or below it.
A window shows as an opening only where the cut passes between its sill and its head.
questions.onCorrect: The plan is cut at 1.2 m because that height passes between the sill and head of ordinary windows. A window with its sill at 1.6 m falls above the cut, so the plan shows the wall unbroken there.

misconceptions.feedback: A plan is a cut. The slice at 1.2 m passes below this sill, so it meets solid wall.
An elevation shows the window from outside, and a section through it would show its height. The plan simply does not cut it.

acceptedIdeas: No opening, because the cut passes below the sill and meets solid wall
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No opening, because the cut passes below the sill and meets solid wall

choices.label: As an opening in the wall, since a plan shows every window in the building
No opening, because the cut passes below the sill and meets solid wall
On no drawing at all, since only an elevation can ever show a window

questions.prompt: A small house has a plan, a section and an elevation. Which drawing shows each of these?
hints: The section is the drawing for heights and build-ups.
The elevation shows only what you could see from outside, with nothing cut.
questions.onCorrect: Each drawing answers a different question, which is why a small building needs all three.

items.label: The width of a room between its walls
items.explanation: The plan is a horizontal cut seen from above, so it gives lengths and widths.

items.label: The direction a door swings
items.explanation: Doors are drawn with their swing on the plan.

items.label: The thickness of the floor
items.explanation: Only the vertical cut passes through the floor.

items.label: The depth of the foundation
items.explanation: It is below ground and hidden from every other drawing.

items.label: The build-up of the roof
items.explanation: Its layers show only where the roof is cut.

items.label: The materials of the outside face
items.explanation: The elevation shows the face as a passer-by sees it.

items.label: The profile of the roof as seen from the street
items.explanation: The outline of the roof is an outside view with nothing cut.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The plan gives the room width and the door swing. The section gives the floor thickness, the foundation depth and the roof build-up. The elevation gives the outside materials and the roof profile.

questions.prompt: A floor plan is drawn at 1:50. You redraw the same plan at 1:100 on a new sheet. What happens to the length of each wall on the paper?
hints: The first number is the drawing and the second is the building.
A larger second number makes the drawing smaller.
questions.onCorrect: Each length on paper is the real length divided by the second number, so changing it from 50 to 100 halves every line. The area on the sheet falls to a quarter.

misconceptions.feedback: A larger second number means more building for each unit of paper, so the drawing shrinks.
The area falls to a quarter, but a length falls only to a half. Length goes with the scale, area with its square.
The label is the scale, and the scale decides how much paper a wall takes. Changing it changes every line.

acceptedIdeas: Every length is halved, as each unit of paper stands for twice as much
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Every length is halved, as each unit of paper stands for twice as much

choices.label: Every length doubles, since the second number has gone up from 50 to 100
Every length drops to a quarter, since the scale number has doubled
Every length is halved, as each unit of paper stands for twice as much
Lengths stay the same, and only the label on the sheet changes

questions.prompt: To size a stair, what do you need to know first?
hints: Which dimension of a stair does not change when you adjust the steps?
The length of a stair depends on the number of steps, and that depends on the rise of each. Ask what fixes the total rise.
questions.onCorrect: The floor-to-floor height is fixed by the storey, and it must be divided into equal risers; the length then follows from the going.

misconceptions.feedback: Length is a result of the arithmetic, not an input. A stair forced into a fixed length gets risers of the wrong height.
Use affects the width of a stair but not the geometry that the height sets.

acceptedIdeas: The height between the two floors
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The height between the two floors

choices.label: The number of people using it
The length that the stair can occupy
The height between the two floors

questions.prompt: Why must the floor-to-floor height be divided into a whole number of risers?
hints: What happens if one riser is taller than the others?
A stair with one riser 20 mm taller than the rest is a tripping hazard. Ask what that says about the risers.
questions.onCorrect: Uneven risers cause missteps, so the height is split into n equal parts, and a whole n near 175 mm each is chosen.

misconceptions.feedback: No code fixes the number of risers. The number follows from the height and the chosen riser.
The going is set by the riser through 2R + G, not by a count of treads.

acceptedIdeas: Every riser must be equal, and a stair cannot have part of a step
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Every riser must be equal, and a stair cannot have part of a step

choices.label: The going is found from the number of treads, which must be whole
Every riser must be equal, and a stair cannot have part of a step
Building codes require an even number of risers

questions.prompt: With a riser of 175 mm and 2R + G = 630 mm, what is the going, in millimetres?
hints: Write the rule with R = 175.
Double the riser first.
Take the doubled riser away from 630 to leave G.
questions.onCorrect: A 175 mm riser with a 280 mm going is a common comfortable pairing, and 2R + G sits in the 550 to 700 mm range of Approved Document K.

misconceptions.feedback: 455 forgets the 2 on the riser. The rule is twice the riser plus the going.
805 adds. The going is what is left of 630 after twice the riser.

questions.prompt: A storey is 2600 mm from floor to floor. You are choosing a whole number of equal risers, aiming near 175 mm and staying within Approved Document K (England, 2013 edition, Table 1.1), which allows a private stair a rise of 150 to 220 mm. Which number of risers suits best?
hints: Divide 2600 by each number and look at the riser it gives.
More than one of them is inside the limits, so choose the one closest to 175 mm.
questions.onCorrect: 2600 ÷ 15 = 173.3 mm, the closest to 175 mm of the four. Whatever number you pick, the risers must all be equal, so the number has to be whole.

misconceptions.feedback: A 200 mm riser is within the limit but steep. Another number gives a riser nearer 175 mm.
A 162.5 mm riser is within the limits but makes a longer, shallower stair than the target. Another number lands nearer 175 mm.
A 185.7 mm riser is allowed, but it is further from 175 mm than the riser that 15 risers give.

acceptedIdeas: 15 risers, each 173.3 mm
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 15 risers, each 173.3 mm

choices.label: 13 risers, each 200 mm
16 risers, each 162.5 mm
14 risers, each 185.7 mm
15 risers, each 173.3 mm

questions.prompt: A storey is 2600 mm floor to floor, climbed in 15 equal risers of 173.33 mm, with the going from 2R + G = 630 mm, so G = 283.33 mm. A flight of 15 risers has 14 goings. The hall can give the stair only 3.6 m of run. By how many millimetres does the stair run beyond the hall, to the nearest millimetre?
hints: The top riser lands on the floor above, so a flight has one fewer going than risers.
Multiply the going by the number of goings to get the run.
Then take away the 3600 mm that the hall allows.
questions.onCorrect: The run is 3967 mm, 367 mm more than the hall gives. The stair has to turn, or the hall has to be lengthened, and it is better to learn that before the plan is drawn.

misconceptions.feedback: 3967 mm is the whole run. The question asks how far it goes past the 3600 mm the hall allows.
That counts 15 goings. A flight of 15 risers has 14 goings, because the top riser lands on the floor above.

questions.prompt: A front door sill stands 450 mm above the path, and the garden gives 8 m along the line of approach. Approved Document M Volume 1 (England, 2015 edition with 2016 amendments) asks for ramp gradients between 1:20 and 1:12, with each flight up to 1:15 no longer than 10 m and each flight up to 1:12 no longer than 5 m. Which ramp does the designer choose?
hints: The length of a ramp is its rise multiplied by the second number of the gradient.
Check each option against both the gradient range and the limit on the length of a flight.
questions.onCorrect: At 1:15 the 450 mm rise needs 6.75 m, which is under the 10 m limit for that gradient and fits the 8 m garden. A short garden does not allow a steeper ramp.

misconceptions.feedback: A flight at 1:12 may be no longer than 5 m, and this one is 5.4 m. It would need a landing and a second flight.
1:10 is steeper than the 1:12 limit, so it is not an acceptable ramp however well it fits the garden.

acceptedIdeas: One flight at 1:15, 6.75 m long
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: One flight at 1:15, 6.75 m long

choices.label: One flight at 1:15, 6.75 m long
One flight at 1:12, 5.4 m in length
One flight at 1:10, 4.5 m long

questions.prompt: A private stair has risers of 210 mm and goings of 210 mm. Which statement is true?
hints: Work out 2R + G first.
Then look at the other limits: pitch and minimum going.
questions.onCorrect: A 210 by 210 stair has a 45 degree pitch and a going under 220 mm, so it breaks two of the limits even though the sum passes.

misconceptions.feedback: 2R + G is only one test. Work out the pitch and compare the going with its minimum before deciding.
2 × 210 + 210 is 630, which is inside the 550 to 700 range.
The riser of 210 mm is within the 220 mm maximum.

acceptedIdeas: 2R + G is 630, but the going and the pitch break their limits
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 2R + G is 630, but the going and the pitch break their limits

choices.label: It fails, because the riser is above the 220 mm limit for stairs
It passes every check, because 2R + G is 630
It fails, because 2R + G is under the 550 minimum
2R + G is 630, but the going and the pitch break their limits

questions.prompt: Above a window opening in a brick wall, the weight of the wall above is carried by
hints: Which part spans the top of the opening?
An opening breaks the wall below it, so something must bridge the gap at its top.
questions.onCorrect: A lintel spans the opening and passes the wall above it to the masonry on each side, so every opening in a wall needs one.

misconceptions.feedback: Glass is not designed to carry load and would crack under it.
The sill is at the bottom of the opening and carries nothing from above it.
A damp-proof course keeps water out of the wall. It is not a beam.

acceptedIdeas: a lintel
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: a lintel

choices.label: the glass
a lintel
the sill
the damp-proof course

questions.prompt: A builder proposes joists at 0.6 m spacing instead of 0.4 m, to save timber. The floor's design load is 2.925 kN/m². What line load does each joist then carry, in kN/m?
hints: Each joist carries a strip of floor as wide as the spacing.
A load per square metre becomes a load per metre when it is multiplied by the width of the strip.
Compare your answer with the 1.17 kN/m the joists carried at 0.4 m.
questions.onCorrect: At 0.6 m each joist carries 1.755 kN/m, 50 percent more than the 1.17 kN/m at 0.4 m, so the timber saved by fewer joists has to be spent on deeper ones.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by the spacing. The strip a joist carries gets wider as the spacing grows, so the load per metre rises in step with it.

questions.prompt: A joist spans 3.0 m and carries 1.17 kN/m. What is the midspan bending moment, in kN m to 2 decimal places?
hints: M = wL² ÷ 8.
Square the span first.
Multiply the line load by that square, then divide by 8.
questions.onCorrect: The span is squared, so shortening a joist from 3.6 m to 3.0 m cuts the moment from 1.90 to 1.32.

misconceptions.feedback: 0.44 uses wL ÷ 8, which forgets to square the span.
3.51 is wL, the total load in kN. The moment divides wL² by 8.

questions.prompt: A floor of 47 × 195 mm joists is a little too weak in bending. You can swap them for 63 × 195 mm joists, which are wider, or for 47 × 245 mm joists, which are deeper. Which gives the larger section modulus Z, and which uses less timber in the cross-section?
hints: Z = bd² ÷ 6, so look at which dimension is squared.
Compare the cross-section areas, b × d, of the two candidates.
questions.onCorrect: The 47 × 245 mm joist has Z = 470.2 cm³ from 11515 mm² of timber, while the 63 × 195 mm joist has 399.3 cm³ from 12285 mm². Depth is squared in Z, so adding depth is the efficient way to resist bending.

misconceptions.feedback: The wider joist has Z = 399.3 cm³ and uses 12285 mm² of timber. The deeper one has more Z from less timber, because depth is squared and width is not.
Z depends only on the shape of the cross-section, b and d. The span changes the moment that Z has to resist.

acceptedIdeas: The deeper joist: Z is 470 cm³ against 399 cm³, with less timber
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The deeper joist: Z is 470 cm³ against 399 cm³, with less timber

choices.label: The deeper joist: Z is 470 cm³ against 399 cm³, with less timber
The wider joist, since more timber across the section always means more strength
Neither changes Z, because Z depends on the span of the joist

questions.prompt: A client's plan has 3.6 m between supports. A 47 × 145 mm joist has Z = 164.7 cm³ and a design bending strength of 7 MPa (illustrative). It carries 1.17 kN/m. What is the longest span it can carry, in metres to one decimal place?
hints: The largest moment it can resist is its Z multiplied by the design strength.
For an even load, M = wL² ÷ 8, so L comes from rearranging this.
Compare the span you find with the 3.6 m the plan needs.
questions.onCorrect: The joist carries 2.8 m, well short of the 3.6 m the plan needs, so it would need to be deeper or the span shortened.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets the square root. M = wL² ÷ 8 gives L² first, and L is its square root.

questions.prompt: A student measures 90 lux on a desk in a bedroom, while an unobstructed outdoor reading under an overcast sky is 6000 lux. What is the daylight factor, in percent?
hints: The daylight factor compares the indoor reading with the outdoor one.
Divide the indoor illuminance by the outdoor illuminance.
The result is a ratio, so it becomes a percentage when you multiply by 100.
questions.onCorrect: 1.5 percent is below the 2 percent that the lesson gives for a room that looks daylit, so this bedroom would want a higher or bigger window, or paler surfaces.

misconceptions.feedback: 0.015 is the ratio. A daylight factor is quoted as a percentage, so multiply by 100.
That divides the outdoor reading by the indoor one. The daylight factor is the indoor reading as a share of the outdoor one.

questions.prompt: Why is a daylight factor defined under an overcast sky?
hints: What does the definition remove from the measurement?
A reading in direct sun would change with the hour and with the way the window faces. Ask what the factor should depend on instead.
questions.onCorrect: Direct sun changes with the hour and the orientation, but an overcast sky is nearly uniform, so the factor describes the room alone.

misconceptions.feedback: Daylight factor does not measure sun. Direct sun is deliberately left out.
An overcast sky is dimmer than a clear one, so brightness cannot be the reason it is used.

acceptedIdeas: The sky is nearly uniform, so the value depends only on the room
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The sky is nearly uniform, so the value depends only on the room

choices.label: The factor measures the sun that enters, which an overcast sky shows most clearly
The sky is nearly uniform, so the value depends only on the room
An overcast sky is the brightest, so it gives the clearest reading

questions.prompt: To bring daylight deeper into a room, which change to the window works best?
hints: Light from high in the window travels farthest back. Which edge is that?

questions.onCorrect: The top of the glass sees the most sky and throws light farthest across the ceiling, so a higher head lights deeper into the room.

misconceptions.feedback: Raising the sill only removes glass at the bottom, where light lands near the window.
A wider window brings in more light overall, but the light still lands in the same places along the floor.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Raise the head of the window

choices.label: Raise the sill of the window
Raise the head of the window
Make the window wider

questions.prompt: A room is 6 m deep and 4.5 m wide, with the window head at 2.1 m. What is L/W + L/Hw, to 2 decimal places?

misconceptions.feedback: 4.03 is the sum for the 5 m by 4 m room with a 1.8 m head. This room is 6 m deep and 4.5 m wide, with the head at 2.1 m.

questions.prompt: A lamp of 400 candela gives 25 lux on a desk 4 m away. You move the desk to 2 m from the lamp, using E = I ÷ d². What illuminance does the desk get?

questions.prompt: A room fails the depth rule L/W + L/Hw ≤ 2/(1 − R). For each change made on its own, does it help the room pass, or make passing harder?
hints: A change helps if it lowers the sum or raises the limit.
L is the depth, W the width, Hw the window head and R the reflectance.
questions.onCorrect: Three things sit in the sum, depth, width and window head, and one in the limit, reflectance. Move any of them and the room's verdict can change.

items.label: Raising the window head
items.explanation: A larger Hw lowers L/Hw, so the sum falls.

items.label: Painting the walls and ceiling white
items.explanation: A larger R raises the limit 2/(1 − R).

items.label: Making the room wider and keeping its depth
items.explanation: A larger W lowers L/W, so the sum falls.

items.label: Making the room deeper
items.explanation: A larger L raises both terms of the sum.

items.label: Lowering the window head
items.explanation: A smaller Hw raises L/Hw, so the sum rises.

items.label: Choosing dark walls and a dark floor
items.explanation: A smaller R lowers the limit.

questions.prompt: A 100 mm layer of brick has a conductivity of 0.77 W/mK, and a 100 mm layer of PIR insulation has 0.022 W/mK. Roughly how does the PIR’s resistance to heat flow compare with the brick’s?
hints: Conductivity says how readily a material passes heat.
Compare 0.77 with 0.022.
questions.onCorrect: At the same thickness, resistance is inversely proportional to conductivity, so the PIR resists about 0.77 ÷ 0.022 = 35 times as much heat flow as the brick.

misconceptions.feedback: Equal thickness does not make equal resistance. The two materials pass heat at very different rates, and their conductivities differ by a factor of about 35.
The conductivities differ by far more than a factor of two: 0.77 is about 35 times 0.022, and the resistances differ by the same factor.
The ratio of the conductivities sets the ratio of the resistances, and 0.77 ÷ 0.022 is about 35, not tens of thousands.

acceptedIdeas: Tens of times more
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Tens of times more

choices.label: About the same, because the two layers are equally thick
Tens of thousands of times more
Tens of times more
A little more, perhaps twice as much

questions.prompt: A wall detail has 100 mm of PIR (conductivity 0.022 W/mK), but the cavity is too tight and you consider mineral wool (0.035 W/mK) instead. What thickness of wool gives the same thermal resistance as the PIR, in millimetres to the nearest millimetre?
hints: Find the resistance of the PIR layer first, in m²K/W.
Resistance is thickness divided by conductivity, so thickness is resistance times conductivity.
Convert the thickness from metres to millimetres at the end.
questions.onCorrect: Wool needs about 159 mm to do the work of 100 mm of PIR, 59 percent more, because its conductivity is that much higher. Where wall thickness costs floor area, PIR is worth its price.

misconceptions.feedback: 100 mm of wool has R = 0.1 ÷ 0.035 = 2.86 m²K/W, only about 63 percent of the PIR's 4.55. A higher conductivity needs more thickness.

questions.prompt: Why are the layers of a wall combined by adding their resistances rather than their U-values?
hints: Think of the layers as steps the heat must pass one after another.

questions.onCorrect: The same heat flow passes through every layer in turn, so each adds its own resistance, and U is the reciprocal of the sum.

misconceptions.feedback: Every U-value is in W/m²K, so the units are not what rules out adding them.
A thick layer of a conductive material can resist less than a thin layer of insulation, and every layer in the path contributes something.

acceptedIdeas: The same heat passes through each layer in turn, so their resistances add
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The same heat passes through each layer in turn, so their resistances add

choices.label: Each layer is measured in its own unit, so U-values cannot be added to each other
The thickest layer decides the result, so only its resistance counts
The same heat passes through each layer in turn, so their resistances add

questions.prompt: Take the PIR out of the wall: the surfaces and the other three layers give a total resistance of 1.23 m²K/W. What is the U-value, in W/m²K to 2 decimal places?
hints: U is the reciprocal of the total resistance.
Divide 1 by the total resistance.
questions.onCorrect: Without the insulation the wall loses about 4.7 times as much heat as the insulated one.

misconceptions.feedback: 1.23 is the resistance. The U-value is its reciprocal.

questions.prompt: A wall of 25 m² with U = 0.173 W/m²K separates air at 20 °C from air at 5 °C. What is the heat loss, in watts to the nearest watt?
hints: Heat loss is U × area × temperature difference.
The temperature difference is 20 − 5.
Multiply the U-value by the area, then by that temperature difference.
questions.onCorrect: The loss is proportional to each of the three factors: doubling the area or the temperature difference doubles the heat lost.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses a temperature difference of 20 K. It is the difference between the two temperatures, 15 K.

questions.prompt: A new house in England has the lesson's wall but with 100 mm of mineral wool in place of the PIR, giving U = 0.244 W/m²K. Approved Document L Volume 1 (2021 edition incorporating 2023 amendments), Table 4.1, gives 0.26 W/m²K as the limiting U-value for a wall in a new dwelling. Its notional dwelling, the reference from which the energy target is set, has 0.18 W/m²K. Which statement is right?
hints: The limiting value is the worst a wall may be. The notional dwelling is a reference for the target.
Compare the wall's U-value with each of the two figures in turn.
questions.onCorrect: The wool wall (0.244) is under the limit and over the notional value, so the design has to find the saving somewhere else, such as better glazing or airtightness. These figures are for England, and other countries set their own.

misconceptions.feedback: 0.18 belongs to the notional dwelling, the reference that sets the energy target. The limit for a wall in a new dwelling is 0.26.
The limit is a minimum standard. Table 4.1 itself notes that some elements need to be significantly better than the limiting standards to meet the target.

acceptedIdeas: It meets the 0.26 limit but not 0.18, so the design must save elsewhere
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It meets the 0.26 limit but not 0.18, so the design must save elsewhere

choices.label: It meets the 0.26 limit but not 0.18, so the design must save elsewhere

questions.prompt: Air at 20 °C and 60 percent relative humidity touches a cold surface. At about what surface temperature does water start to form?
hints: Cooling air raises its relative humidity without changing how much vapour it holds.
At 60 percent humidity the air is some way from saturated. It would take several degrees of cooling, but not freezing.
questions.onCorrect: The dew point of 20 °C air at 60 percent humidity is 12.0 °C, so any surface colder than that collects water.

misconceptions.feedback: Water does not form on a surface at that temperature, because the air touching it has not been cooled enough.
A surface that is barely cooler than the room is still far above the saturation point of this air.
Freezing is not involved: water condenses as soon as a surface falls below the saturation temperature of the air next to it.

questions.prompt: Two houses each have a volume of 200 m³. One is leaky, at 2.0 air changes an hour, and the other is tighter, at 0.5. With 20 K between inside and outside, how many more watts does the leaky house need to heat its air? Use H = 0.33 n V.
hints: Work out H in W/K for each house.
Take the difference in H, then multiply by the temperature difference.
The answer is a power, so it should be in watts and not W/K.
questions.onCorrect: The leaky house needs about 2 kW more, all day and night, just to warm air that comes in through gaps. Sealing the building comes before enlarging the heating.

misconceptions.feedback: 99 is the difference in W/K. Multiply by the 20 K between inside and outside to get watts.

questions.prompt: A concrete lintel bridges the insulation and has a local U-value of 1.2 W/m²K (illustrative). With 20 °C inside and 0 °C outside and Rsi = 0.13, what is its inside surface temperature, in °C to 2 decimal places?
hints: Use the same formula as for the wall, with the lintel's own U-value: Ts = Ti − U × Rsi × ΔT.
Work out how far the surface falls below the room temperature.
Take that fall away from the 20 °C inside.
questions.onCorrect: This cold spot is colder than the wall around it by 2.7 degrees, so mould and condensation start there first when the air is humid.

misconceptions.feedback: 3.12 is the temperature drop. Subtract it from 20.
19.55 is the plain wall. The lintel conducts more heat, so it is colder.

questions.prompt: A room has its air at 20 °C and its walls at 16 °C. Roughly how warm will the room feel to a person sitting in it?
hints: Heat leaves a person both to the air and to the surfaces in view.
Which of the two is colder here?
questions.onCorrect: With still air the felt temperature is close to the average of the air and the surfaces, (20 + 16) ÷ 2 = 18 °C, two degrees below the thermometer reading.

misconceptions.feedback: The air temperature is only part of it. The person also radiates heat to the cold walls, so the room feels cooler than the thermometer says.
The body’s own heat is what is being lost, and it is lost faster to cold walls, so the room feels cooler than 20 °C rather than warmer.
The walls are only part of it. The air at 20 °C also takes heat from the body.

acceptedIdeas: About 18 °C, the average of the air and the walls
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 18 °C, the average of the air and the walls

choices.label: About 20 °C, the temperature of the air in the room
About 22 °C, because the body adds its own heat
About 16 °C, the temperature of the walls
About 18 °C, the average of the air and the walls

questions.prompt: A seminar room holds 20 people sitting at 1.2 met. One met is 58.2 W per m² of skin, and each person has 1.8 m² of skin. How much heat do the people give off together, in watts to the nearest watt?
hints: One person gives off the met value times 58.2 W/m² times their skin area.
Work out one person's heat in watts first.
Then multiply by the number of people.
questions.onCorrect: About 2.5 kW, the output of a small heater. A full seminar room can overheat while its heating is off, which is why the people count in the heat balance.

misconceptions.feedback: 126 W is one person. The room has twenty.

questions.prompt: A thermostat in a living room reads 20 °C. A person sitting beside a large single-glazed window, whose inner surface is at 8 °C, feels cold. Which explanation fits?
hints: Comfort depends on the surfaces around a person as well as the air.
The body loses heat by radiation to every cooler surface in view.

misconceptions.feedback: Air temperature is one of six factors. The mean radiant temperature of the surfaces around a person matters as much.

questions.prompt: At latitude 40 degrees north the June noon altitude is 73.44 degrees. A south window has its head 0.3 m below a 0.5 m overhang and its sill 1.5 m below it. How far down the wall does the overhang shade at noon in June, in metres to two decimal places? Use depth = overhang × tan(altitude).
hints: The shadow depth is the overhang's projection times tan(altitude).
Compute 0.5 × tan 73.44°.
Compare the depth with the 1.5 m to the sill.

questions.prompt: A passive design works with the sun in both seasons. Which of these actions serves the winter aim, and which the summer aim?

questions.prompt: Why is the tangent of the pitch the right ratio for finding the rise?

questions.prompt: On a plan, one wall carries dimension strings of 5000 and 3500 in the first tier, and the overall string reads 8000. What should the builder do?

misconceptions.feedback: Measuring a print is the least reliable way to settle it, and builders are told to use stated dimensions in preference.

questions.prompt: On a plan, a 2.4 m wide bathroom has its door drawn with an arc that sweeps across the middle of the room, into the 1.5 m circle kept clear for turning a wheelchair. What does the plan show?

misconceptions.feedback: The arc also shows the space the leaf sweeps, and that space must stay clear of anything the room needs, including the turning circle.
A 2.4 m room holds a 1.5 m circle easily. The fault is the way the door is hung, and hanging it the other way clears the circle.

acceptedIdeas: The door swings into the clear circle, so the room cannot be used
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The door swings into the clear circle, so the room cannot be used

The door swings into the clear circle, so the room cannot be used

questions.prompt: A house 9 m by 6 m is to be drawn on one landscape A3 sheet, which is 420 × 297 mm, leaving 40 mm margins all round. Which is the largest of these scales that fits?
hints: The area inside the margins is 340 × 217 mm.

questions.onCorrect: At 1:50 the house is 180 × 120 mm, inside the 340 × 217 mm area. The same division, real length over the second number of the scale, gives any line.

misconceptions.feedback: 1:100 fits, at 90 × 60 mm, but a larger scale also fits.

questions.prompt: The client asks for the cabin to be 7 m long instead of 6 m, keeping its 4 m width. The cost is 2200 per m² of gross area (an illustrative rate) and the efficiency is 85 percent. What does the extra metre do?
hints: The extra metre adds to the footprint, and the footprint is the gross area.
Only part of the extra gross area becomes usable room.
questions.onCorrect: The extra 4 m² is gross area and costs 8,800. At 85 percent efficiency 3.4 m² of it is usable room, so the client pays for floor they cannot use.

misconceptions.feedback: Cost follows the gross area, which is all built. The extra 4 m² costs 8,800, even though less of it is usable.
Only 85 percent of the gross area is usable room. The rest goes to walls and circulation.

acceptedIdeas: It adds 4 m² of floor and 8,800, of which 3.4 m² is usable
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It adds 4 m² of floor and 8,800, of which 3.4 m² is usable

choices.label: It adds 4 m² of floor and 8,800, of which 3.4 m² is usable
It adds 3.4 m² and 7,480 to the cost, because cost follows the usable area
It adds 4 m² of room and 8,800 to the cost, with all of it usable

questions.prompt: The client asks to turn the cabin a quarter turn, so that its 4 m end faces south and the long wall faces east. The main room is then 6 m deep from south to north and 4 m wide, with its window head at 2.1 m and surfaces at R = 0.5, so the limit is 4. What does the depth rule give?
hints: L is the depth from the window wall to the back wall, which is now the longer dimension.
Work out L/W + L/Hw and compare it with 4.
questions.onCorrect: 6/4 + 6/2.1 = 4.36, over the limit, so the back of the room would be dim. A 4 m south wall also has less room for glazing than the 6 m one, which is why the long wall faces the sun.

misconceptions.feedback: The room is the same size, but L is now 6 m and W is 4 m, so the sum changes.
The depth rule works for any room with a window wall. It takes the depth, width and window head.

acceptedIdeas: 4.36, over the limit of 4, and the south wall now has less room for glass
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 4.36, over the limit of 4, and the south wall now has less room for glass

choices.label: 4.36, over the limit of 4, and the south wall now has less room for glass
2.57, as before, since the room is the same size and has only changed direction
It cannot be found, because the rule applies only to south-facing rooms

questions.prompt: The cabin’s walls have a net area of 44 m² and U = 0.173 W/m²K. What is their heat-loss rate UA, in W/K to 1 decimal place?
hints: UA is the U-value times the area.
The area is 44 m².
Multiply the U-value by the wall area.
questions.onCorrect: The wall area is the gross wall area minus the glazing, because the windows have their own U-value.

misconceptions.feedback: 8.3 uses the gross wall area of 48 m². Subtract the 4 m² of glazing.

questions.prompt: With triple glazing the cabin's heat-loss routes in W/K are walls 7.6, glazing 3.2, roof 2.9, floor 3.6 and ventilation 9.5, a total of 26.8. Where does the next effort do most good?
hints: Look for the largest single route.
Sealing a house cuts the loss, but the people in it still need fresh air.
questions.onCorrect: Ventilation is 9.5 of 26.8 W/K, more than the walls at 7.6. The usual answer is to make the cabin airtight and ventilate it deliberately, recovering heat from the outgoing air.

misconceptions.feedback: The walls already have U = 0.173 and lose 7.6 W/K, less than ventilation. More insulation here buys little.
Two occupants breathe, cook and wash, and that moisture has to leave. The answer is to seal it and then ventilate on purpose.

acceptedIdeas: Airtightness plus heat-recovery ventilation, since ventilation is the largest route
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Airtightness plus heat-recovery ventilation, since ventilation is the largest route

choices.label: More wall insulation, since the walls are where insulation is usually spent first
Airtightness plus heat-recovery ventilation, since ventilation is the largest route
Seal the cabin completely and remove ventilation, since all the air leaving takes heat

questions.prompt: Fit only a thin layer of insulation in the cabin’s walls, so that their U-value is 0.45 W/m²K. The walls are 44 m², and the other losses stay at 21.6 W/K. What heating power does the cabin then need at 20 K, in watts to the nearest watt?
hints: First recompute the wall loss with U = 0.45.
Add the rest, 21.6.
Multiply the total by 20.
questions.onCorrect: The heater would have to be about 40 percent larger, which is why the fabric is improved before systems are added.

misconceptions.feedback: 584 W is the fully insulated cabin. The thinly insulated walls lose more.
41.4 is the loss in W/K. Multiply by 20 K for watts.
1144 W is the cabin with no wall insulation at all. Here the walls have U = 0.45.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Walls: 44 × 0.45 = 19.8 W/K. Total = 19.8 + 21.6 = 41.4 W/K, and at 20 K that is 828 W.

questions.prompt: A 9 m wall stands at latitude 50 degrees north, where the noon sun altitude on 21 December is 16.56 degrees. How long is the wall’s noon shadow, in metres to the nearest metre?
hints: tan(altitude) = wall height ÷ shadow length.
Rearrange to shadow = height ÷ tan(altitude), with your calculator in degree mode.
Find tan of 16.56 degrees, then divide the wall's height by it.
questions.onCorrect: 9 ÷ tan 16.56° = 9 ÷ 0.2974 = 30.3, so the shadow is about 30 m, more than three times the height of the wall.

misconceptions.feedback: About 2.7 m comes from multiplying 9 by tan 16.56°. The tangent is height over shadow, so the shadow is the height divided by it.
About 10.7 m uses the equinox altitude of 40 degrees. On 21 December the declination lowers it to 16.56 degrees.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Shadow = 9 ÷ tan 16.56° = 9 ÷ 0.2974 = 30.3, which is 30 m to the nearest metre.

questions.prompt: The room air has a dew point of 13.2 °C, and the inside surface of an insulated wall is at 19.55 °C. What happens on that surface?
hints: Compare the surface temperature with the dew point. Which one is lower?

questions.onCorrect: Water forms only where a surface is colder than the dew point, and this wall is more than six degrees warmer than it.

misconceptions.feedback: Condensation needs a surface colder than the dew point. At 19.55 °C this wall is well above 13.2 °C, so the air beside it never reaches saturation.
Freezing needs a temperature below 0 °C, and this surface is at 19.55 °C.
The two temperatures are enough: a surface above the dew point stays dry.

acceptedIdeas: The surface stays dry
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The surface stays dry

choices.label: The surface stays dry
The water freezes
There is not enough information
Condensation forms

questions.prompt: A concrete lintel bridges the insulation, and its inside surface is at 16.88 °C while the plain wall beside it is at 19.55 °C. On a humid day the room air’s dew point rises to 17.5 °C. What happens?
hints: Compare each surface with the new dew point.
Only a surface colder than 17.5 °C collects water.
questions.onCorrect: The damp appears along the line of the bridge first, which is why a cold lintel shows as a dark stripe above a window long before the rest of the wall is affected.

misconceptions.feedback: The plain wall, at 19.55 °C, is warmer than the 17.5 °C dew point, so it stays dry. The lintel is the colder of the two surfaces.
Water forms on any surface colder than the dew point, not only below freezing. The lintel, at 16.88 °C, is below 17.5 °C.
The room air is at 20 °C, but what matters is each surface’s own temperature. The lintel, at 16.88 °C, is below the dew point.

acceptedIdeas: Water forms on the lintel while the plain wall stays dry
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Water forms on the lintel while the plain wall stays dry

choices.label: Water forms on the plain wall but not on the lintel
Both stay dry, since both surfaces are well above 0 °C
Both stay dry, since the room air itself is as warm as 20 °C
Water forms on the lintel while the plain wall stays dry

questions.prompt: Why is the heat a person gives off found by multiplying the met value by the area of their skin?
hints: Look at the unit of one met.
A quantity per square metre becomes a total when it is multiplied by the number of square metres.
questions.onCorrect: Because a met is a rate per square metre, a larger person doing the same work gives off proportionally more heat.

misconceptions.feedback: The skin area does not change the units from degrees to watts. A met is already in watts, per square metre of skin.
The calculation does not depend on how warm the person feels. It counts the heat produced, which is a rate per square metre of skin.

acceptedIdeas: A met is a rate of heat per square metre of skin, so the total grows with area
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A met is a rate of heat per square metre of skin, so the total grows with area

choices.label: Multiplying by the skin area converts degrees into watts, which are the unit of heat
A met is a rate of heat per square metre of skin, so the total grows with area
A person with more skin feels warmer, so more heat has to be counted for them

questions.prompt: A drawing labelled 1:100 was made on A1 and has been printed at 50 percent on A3. A dimension string on the print reads 4200. What should the builder trust?

misconceptions.feedback: The label does not shrink with the print, so it is wrong once the sheet is halved. The print is now at 1:200.

acceptedIdeas: The stated 4200, since the print is now at 1:200, not 1:100

The stated 4200, since the print is now at 1:200, not 1:100

questions.prompt: Two identical houses stand at latitude 35 degrees, one north of the equator and one south of it. Which house does each statement describe?
hints: Decide where the noon sun stands in each hemisphere before you read the statements.
In winter the noon sun is low, and it stands on the equator side of the house.
questions.onCorrect: The advice to face the equator holds in both hemispheres, and it points to a different wall in each.

items.label: The December noon sun is high in the north

items.label: The wall that collects winter sun is the south wall

questions.prompt: The studio has 34 m² of net area and 40 m² of gross area. At 2200 per m², what does it cost to build?
hints: Think about which area the builder has to build.
The studio's rooms are 34 m², but the building also holds walls, an entry and services.
Multiply that area by 2200.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The cost is charged on the gross area: 40 × 2200 = 88 000.

questions.onCorrect: The studio costs 88 000 even though only 34 m² of it is rooms, because the 6 m² of walls, entry and services is built and paid for too.

misconceptions.feedback: 74 800 charges the rate on the 34 m² of rooms. The walls, entry and services are built too.

questions.prompt: A family with a toddler wants the parent who is cooking to keep an eye on the child playing in the living room. In a bubble diagram, which pair of spaces most needs a direct link?
hints: Ask which two spaces the parent moves between, or looks across, throughout the day.
The child has to be seen from where the parent cooks. Ask which two spaces those two people are in.

acceptedIdeas: Kitchen and living room
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Kitchen and living room

questions.onCorrect: The parent and the child need to see and reach each other all day, so the shortest path between kitchen and living room is the one to design.

choices.label: Kitchen and living room
Store and bedroom 2
Dining room and bedroom 1
Bathroom and entrance

misconceptions.feedback: A store is visited now and then, so few trips are made between it and a bedroom.
Few trips are made between a dining room and a bedroom, and nothing in this family’s day connects them.
A bathroom door that opens on the front step is an arrangement most clients refuse, so a plan avoids that link.

questions.prompt: A student works out the 6.5 m wall at 1:100 and gets 650 000 mm for its length on paper. What did the student do?
hints: Work out what each slip would give, and see which one produces 650 000.
A 6.5 m wall is 6500 mm. At 1:100 its length on paper should be smaller than the wall.

acceptedIdeas: Multiplied by 100 instead of dividing
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Multiplied by 100 instead of dividing

questions.onCorrect: 6500 × 100 = 650 000, so the student scaled the wall up instead of down. The check in the line above catches this, because a drawing of a building is smaller than the building.

choices.label: Used the 1:50 scale instead of 1:100
Multiplied by 100 instead of dividing
Forgot to change metres to millimetres

misconceptions.feedback: At 1:50 the length on paper would be 130 mm, a small number and nothing like 650 000.
Dividing 6.5 by 100 without converting gives 0.065, which is a tiny number.

questions.prompt: You are sizing a private stair between two floors 2700 mm apart. In what order do you work?
hints: The riser height cannot be found until the number of risers is fixed.
The going comes from the comfort rule, and the run from the going.
questions.onCorrect: Each number feeds the next, and the check against the code comes last because it needs the finished rise and going.

items: Measure the floor-to-floor height
Choose a whole number of risers that puts each riser near 175 mm
Divide the height by the number of risers to get the riser
Find the going from 2R + G = 630 mm
Multiply the going by the number of goings to get the run
Check the rise, going and pitch against Approved Document K

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: With 2700 mm the lesson chooses 16 risers, so R = 168.75 mm, G = 292.5 mm and the run is 15 × 292.5 = 4387.5 mm, with a pitch of 30.0 degrees. The height comes first because every later number depends on it, and the check comes last because it needs the finished dimensions.

questions.prompt: Four private stairs are proposed for houses in England. Using Approved Document K (2013 edition, Table 1.1), a private stair has a rise of 150 to 220 mm, a going of 220 to 300 mm and a pitch of no more than 42 degrees. Which one fails?
hints: Check the rise and the going of each stair against their ranges first.
The pitch is the angle whose tangent is the rise divided by the going.
questions.onCorrect: The 210 mm going is under the 220 mm minimum, and the pitch is 43.6 degrees, over the 42 degree limit. Its 2R + G is 610 mm, which looks fine, so the sum alone cannot clear a stair.

misconceptions.feedback: Rise and going are inside their ranges, and the pitch is 33.9 degrees, so it passes.
The going of 300 mm is at the top of its range and the pitch is 28.1 degrees, so it passes.
Rise and going are inside their ranges, 2R + G is 630 mm and the pitch is 37.2 degrees, so it passes.

acceptedIdeas: Rise 200 mm, going 210 mm
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Rise 200 mm, going 210 mm
