Rise 160 mm, going 300 mm
Rise 190 mm, going 250 mm

questions.prompt: A plan for a small house has the living room off the hall, the kitchen off the living room, bedroom 1 off the hall and the bathroom off the hall. The only way into bedroom 2 is through bedroom 1. What is wrong with the circulation?
hints: Trace the route a visitor or a child takes to reach each room.
Circulation should reach every room without crossing another private one.
questions.onCorrect: Circulation exists so that every room is reached without passing through another one. A route through bedroom 1 takes away its privacy, and the plan should give bedroom 2 its own door onto the hall.

misconceptions.feedback: A kitchen reached through a living room is a common and workable arrangement. The fault in this plan is the route to bedroom 2.
Halls count in the gross area and are rightly drawn. They are circulation, which every plan needs.

acceptedIdeas: Anyone going to bedroom 2 has to cross bedroom 1, a private room
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Anyone going to bedroom 2 has to cross bedroom 1, a private room

choices.label: The kitchen is reached through the living room, and the hall should reach every room
Anyone going to bedroom 2 has to cross bedroom 1, a private room
The hall counts as net area, and it should not have been drawn

questions.prompt: Why does the imposed load get a larger factor than the dead load?
hints: Ask which of the two loads you can predict better before the building is used.
The dead load is the floor's own weight, which can be calculated. Ask what can be said about the weight of people and furniture.

acceptedIdeas: People and furniture are less predictable than the structure’s own weight
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: People and furniture are less predictable than the structure’s own weight

questions.onCorrect: The floor’s own weight can be calculated, but how many people stand on it and what they bring cannot, so the imposed load gets the larger factor.

choices.label: The imposed load is the larger of the two loads, so it needs the larger factor
The factors are chosen so that both loads count equally in the total
People and furniture are less predictable than the structure’s own weight

misconceptions.feedback: A factor allows for how uncertain a load is, whatever its size. The imposed load happens to be larger here, and that is not what raises its factor.
The factors do not balance the loads: 1.35 × 0.5 = 0.675 against 1.5 × 1.5 = 2.25, so the imposed load counts for far more in the total.

questions.prompt: A person stands on the first floor of a house with brick walls. In what order does their weight pass to the ground?
hints: The load travels from what is loaded towards what is stiffest and lowest.
A joist rests on a wall, and a wall rests on something that spreads its load.
questions.onCorrect: The load path must be continuous. A load that reaches a point with nothing below it will bend or break whatever is there.

items: The floor boards
A floor joist
The wall that the joist ends rest on
The foundation under the wall
The soil beneath the foundation

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The weight goes from the boards into the joist, from the joist into the wall it rests on, from the wall into its foundation and from the foundation into the soil, which has to be wide enough to hold it.

questions.prompt: A designer is checking which walls in a house can be altered. Which of these carry load from above, and which carry only their own weight?
hints: Ask what rests on the wall: joist ends, rafters, a floor above or a wall above.
A wall that nothing rests on carries only itself.
questions.onCorrect: A wall is load-bearing when something rests on it, whatever its thickness or position.

items.label: An outside wall that the roof rafters rest on
items.explanation: The roof's weight passes down through it.

items.label: An inside wall under the ends of the first-floor joists
items.explanation: The floor above bears on it.

items.label: The lintel over a window in a wall that carries the floor above
items.explanation: It passes the wall's load round the opening.

items.label: A partition that runs parallel to the joists and has nothing resting on it
items.explanation: No joist ends or wall rest on it, so it supports only itself.

items.label: A thin partition in a bungalow whose roof truss spans from outside wall to outside wall
items.explanation: The truss rests on the outside walls and not on the partition.

items.label: A glazed screen between the kitchen and the hall with nothing above it
items.explanation: Nothing bears on it, so it carries only its own weight.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The outside wall under the rafters, the inside wall under the joist ends and the lintel over the window carry load from above. The parallel partition, the partition under the spanning truss and the glazed screen carry only themselves.

questions.prompt: A client wants to take out the wall between the kitchen and the living room to make one open room. The first-floor joists run across the house and rest on that wall. What do you check before agreeing?
hints: Think about the load path through that wall.
Removing a wall removes whatever it was holding up.
questions.onCorrect: The joists rest on this wall, so removing it needs a beam with its own support to carry the floor above, sized for the load that the wall carried.

misconceptions.feedback: Thickness does not decide it. What rests on a wall decides, and a thin wall can carry a floor.
Inside walls often carry the ends of joists. The joists here rest on this one, so it carries the floor above.

acceptedIdeas: What the wall carries, and what will carry it once the wall has gone
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: What the wall carries, and what will carry it once the wall has gone

choices.label: What the wall carries, and what will carry it once the wall has gone
How thick the wall is, since thick walls carry load and thin ones do not
Whether it is an inside wall, because inside walls carry nothing

questions.prompt: A room 5 m deep and 4 m wide has its window head at 1.8 m, so L/W + L/Hw = 4.03. With pale surfaces (R = 0.6, limit 5) it passes the depth rule. A tenant repaints it in dark colours so that R falls to 0.3. What happens?
hints: Ask which side of the rule the reflectance appears on.
Work out the new limit 2/(1 − R) and compare it with the sum.
questions.onCorrect: At R = 0.3 the limit is 2 ÷ 0.7 = 2.9, and the sum is unchanged at 4.03, so the room that passed with pale walls now fails by a wide margin.

misconceptions.feedback: The sum depends on the room's depth, width and window head, and paint does not change those. Paint changes the limit.
The limit is 2/(1 − R), so it depends on the reflectance. Darker surfaces lower R and with it the limit.

acceptedIdeas: The limit falls to 2.9 while the sum stays at 4.03, so the room fails
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The limit falls to 2.9 while the sum stays at 4.03, so the room fails

choices.label: The sum falls, so the room passes more easily
The limit falls to 2.9 while the sum stays at 4.03, so the room fails
The limit stays at 5, since the limit depends on the size of the room

questions.prompt: A bedroom is 5 m deep and 3.5 m wide, with its window head at 2.4 m. What is L/W + L/Hw, to 2 decimal places? At R = 0.5 the limit is 4.
hints: L is the depth from the window wall to the back wall.
Work out L/W and L/Hw separately.
Add the two, then compare the sum with the limit of 4.
questions.onCorrect: 3.51 is below the limit of 4, so the bedroom passes the depth rule at R = 0.5.

questions.prompt: A room 6 m deep and 4.5 m wide has its window head at 2.1 m, and its depth sum of 4.19 is over the limit of 4. Which change brings the room within the limit?
hints: Work out the new sum for each change and compare it with 4.
The depth L is in both terms of the sum. Ask which changes lower the sum and which raise it.

acceptedIdeas: Raise the head to 2.4 m
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Raise the head to 2.4 m

questions.onCorrect: With the head at 2.4 m the sum falls to 6 ÷ 4.5 + 6 ÷ 2.4 = 3.83, under the limit of 4.

choices.label: Lower the head to 1.8 m
Make the room 0.5 m deeper
Paint the surfaces a darker colour
Raise the head to 2.4 m

misconceptions.feedback: At 1.8 m, L/Hw rises to 3.33 and the sum to 4.67, further over the limit.
A deeper room raises both terms. At 6.5 m deep the sum is 4.54.
Darker surfaces lower the reflectance R, and that lowers the limit 2 ÷ (1 − R) below 4.

questions.prompt: A builder offers two walls for a small extension: 440 mm of solid brick (conductivity 0.77 W/mK, U = 1.35 W/m²K), or the lesson's wall of 102 mm brick, 100 mm PIR, 100 mm block and 13 mm plaster (U = 0.173). Which loses less heat, and why?
hints: Compare the total resistance of each wall before you look at its thickness.
Work out how much brick has the resistance of 100 mm of PIR.
questions.onCorrect: The brick wall has R = 0.74 m²K/W and U = 1.35, about eight times the insulated wall's 0.173, because 100 mm of PIR (R = 4.55) does the work of 3.5 m of brick.

misconceptions.feedback: Thickness does not decide it. Resistance is thickness divided by conductivity, and brick conducts about 35 times as readily as PIR.
U is a property of the wall's layers. The temperatures only decide how much heat flows once U is known.

acceptedIdeas: The insulated wall, because its PIR resists as much as 3.5 m of brick
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The insulated wall, because its PIR resists as much as 3.5 m of brick

choices.label: The insulated wall, because its PIR resists as much as 3.5 m of brick
The solid brick wall, because at 440 mm it is thicker than the other at 315 mm
They lose the same, because U depends only on the temperatures either side

questions.prompt: A 30 m² wall faces outside air at 3 °C, and the room behind it is at 21 °C. With its PIR the wall has U = 0.173 W/m²K, and with the PIR left out it has U = 0.81. How many more watts does the wall lose without the insulation, to the nearest watt?
hints: Heat loss is U × A × ΔT, so find ΔT first.
Work out the loss for each U-value, or the difference in U first.
Take the smaller loss from the larger.
questions.onCorrect: Leaving the PIR out costs about 344 W through this one wall, nearly five times what the insulated wall loses, and the cost comes back every hour of the heating season.

misconceptions.feedback: 93 W is the loss with the insulation in place. The question asks for the extra loss when it is left out.

questions.prompt: A client says that doubling the PIR in the lesson's wall from 100 mm to 200 mm will halve the heat lost through it. The wall's U-value is now 0.173 W/m²K. Roughly what does the U-value become?
hints: Only one layer changes. The other layers and the surface films keep their resistance.
Add the extra resistance of 100 mm of PIR to the total and invert again.
questions.onCorrect: The total resistance rises from 5.78 to 10.33 m²K/W, so U falls from 0.173 to 0.097, a drop of 44 percent. Each extra layer of insulation helps less than the one before it.

misconceptions.feedback: U is the inverse of the total resistance. Only the PIR layer doubles, and the other layers and films stay as they were, so the total does not double.
The PIR provides most of the wall's resistance, so a second 100 mm adds nearly as much again.

acceptedIdeas: It falls by about 44 percent, to 0.097, because the other layers do not change
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It falls by about 44 percent, to 0.097, because the other layers do not change

choices.label: It falls by about 44 percent, to 0.097, because the other layers do not change
It falls to 0.087, since U is inversely proportional to the thickness of the insulation
It falls by about 10 percent, since the first 100 mm does almost all the work

questions.prompt: Why does water form on a surface that is colder than the dew point of the room air?
hints: Think about what happens to the air that touches the cold surface.
Cold air holds less vapour than warm air. Ask what happens to the vapour in air that is chilled.

acceptedIdeas: The air touching it is cooled to saturation, so it deposits vapour
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The air touching it is cooled to saturation, so it deposits vapour

questions.onCorrect: Cooling the air next to the surface raises its relative humidity to 100 percent, and the vapour it can no longer hold collects as water.

choices.label: The cold surface draws moisture through the wall from outside
The air touching it is cooled to saturation, so it deposits vapour
Humid air leaves water on every surface it touches, whatever the temperature

misconceptions.feedback: Water that passes through a wall is a leak or rising damp, which is a different problem from condensation.
Temperature matters as well as humidity: the warm inside face of an insulated wall stays dry in the same air.

questions.prompt: Heat leaves a small house by two kinds of route. Which of these lose heat through the fabric, and which with moving air?
hints: Heat conducted through a solid layer is fabric loss, whatever the layer is.
If warm air itself leaves and cold air replaces it, that is ventilation loss.
questions.onCorrect: Fabric loss depends on U-values and areas, and air loss on how often the air is replaced. A building needs both kept low.

items.label: Conduction through the layers of an external wall
items.explanation: The heat passes through solid layers, so the U-value governs it.

items.label: Conduction through the glass of a window
items.explanation: The glazing's U-value governs it.

items.label: A concrete lintel that crosses the wall's insulation
items.explanation: It is a thermal bridge, a fabric route that conducts better than the wall around it.

items.label: Conduction through the roof insulation
items.explanation: The roof's U-value governs it.

items.label: Warm air leaving through gaps around a loft hatch
items.explanation: The air itself carries the heat out, and cold air has to be warmed to replace it.

items.label: Cold air drawn in under the front door
items.explanation: It is an air change, counted in H = 0.33 n V.

items.label: Air carried out by a bathroom extract fan
items.explanation: It is deliberate ventilation, and it takes warmed air with it.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Conduction through the wall, the glass, the lintel and the roof insulation is fabric loss. The loft hatch gaps, the draught under the door and the extract fan lose heat with moving air.

questions.prompt: A couple insulate their old house thickly and seal every gap they can find. The next winter there is mould on the bedroom walls. What is the most likely missing piece?
hints: Think about where the moisture that people make goes once the leaks are closed.
Sealing cuts ventilation loss, but ventilation also removed something.
questions.onCorrect: People breathe, cook and wash, and that moisture has to leave. The usual answer is to make the building airtight and then ventilate it on purpose, often with heat recovery.

misconceptions.feedback: Mould needs moisture as well as a cool surface, and the sealed house has trapped the moisture its occupants make.
Airtightness does not cause mould. A tight building with deliberate ventilation, often with heat recovery, avoids both draughts and damp.

acceptedIdeas: Deliberate ventilation, since the moisture they make has nowhere to go
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Deliberate ventilation, since the moisture they make has nowhere to go

choices.label: More insulation, since mould grows only on walls that are cold enough
Deliberate ventilation, since the moisture they make has nowhere to go
Fewer seals, since making a house airtight always causes mould to grow

questions.prompt: The room air has a dew point of 14 °C. Which of these inside surfaces collects water?
hints: Compare each surface temperature with 14 °C.
Only surfaces colder than the dew point matter. Cross out any that are warmer.

acceptedIdeas: A glass pane at 13.5 °C
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A glass pane at 13.5 °C

questions.onCorrect: Only the glass is colder than the dew point, so the air touching it is cooled to saturation and deposits water.

choices.label: A plain wall at 19.0 °C
A lintel at 15.2 °C
A glass pane at 13.5 °C
A floor at 17.0 °C

misconceptions.feedback: At 19.0 °C the wall is above the dew point, so the air next to it never reaches saturation.
The lintel is the coldest part of the wall, but at 15.2 °C it is still warmer than the dew point, so it stays dry.
At 17.0 °C the floor is above the dew point, so it stays dry.

questions.prompt: A room has a heavy stone floor that was in the sun until 4 pm. At 9 pm the sun is gone and the room air is cooling. What is the floor doing?
hints: Think about what a heavy stone floor holds after a day in the sun.
Ask whether the floor is warmer or cooler than the air at 9 pm after hours in the sun.

acceptedIdeas: Releasing heat it absorbed while the sun was on it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Releasing heat it absorbed while the sun was on it

questions.onCorrect: A heavy floor evens out swings: it absorbs heat from the sun by day and gives it back at night, so it helps in winter and in summer.

choices.label: Making new heat from the sunlight that is stored in it
Cooling the room, because stone is always cold
Releasing heat it absorbed while the sun was on it
Shading the room from the low evening sun

misconceptions.feedback: Mass makes no heat of its own. It can only give back heat that it absorbed.
Stone feels cold to the touch because it carries heat away from the hand, but after a sunny day the floor is warmer than the evening air.
Shading is done by an overhang or a blind. Mass absorbs and delays heat, and at 9 pm there is no sun to block.

questions.prompt: A room with a heavy stone floor reaches 28 °C by the evening of a hot day, and the night air outside falls to 14 °C. What helps the room most the next day?
hints: Thermal mass stores heat when the room is warm and releases it when the room is cool.
To absorb heat again tomorrow, the mass has to give up what it holds.
questions.onCorrect: Ventilating at night when the air is cool lets the mass shed the day's heat, and it can absorb heat again the next afternoon. Mass is a battery, and it has to be discharged to be useful.

misconceptions.feedback: After a hot day the stone is warm. Shutting the windows keeps its heat in and leaves it nothing to absorb tomorrow.
Mass does not make heat. It smooths the swings, so a light floor would let the room heat up faster.

acceptedIdeas: Open the windows at night so the cool air draws heat out of the floor
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Open the windows at night so the cool air draws heat out of the floor

choices.label: Open the windows at night so the cool air draws heat out of the floor
Keep the windows shut all night so the stone's coolness stays in
Swap the stone floor for a light one, since mass is what makes rooms hot

questions.prompt: A roof is 6 m by 8 m in plan and pitched at 45 degrees, so its sloping surface is 67.9 m². Rain falls at 60 mm/h. How much water reaches the gutters in an hour?
hints: Rain falls straight down. Ask which area the sky sees.
One millimetre of rain on one square metre is one litre.
questions.onCorrect: The flow is the rainfall intensity times the plan area, 60 × 48 = 2880 litres an hour. The slope decides how fast the water leaves the roof, and the plan area decides how much arrives.

misconceptions.feedback: The sloping surface is larger than the area the sky sees, and rain falls straight down. A steeper roof does not catch more.
That changes the plan area when it is already the right one. The plan area, 48 m², is what the rain meets.

acceptedIdeas: 2,880 litres, because only the 48 m² of plan area catches falling rain
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 2,880 litres, because only the 48 m² of plan area catches falling rain

choices.label: 4,073 litres, because the sloping surface is the area the rain lands on
2,036 litres, found by multiplying the plan area by cos 45°
2,880 litres, because only the 48 m² of plan area catches falling rain

questions.prompt: A damp-proof course sits 150 mm above the ground along a wall. The owner lays a patio that raises the ground beside the wall by 90 mm. What follows?
hints: Work out how far above the new ground the course sits.
The course must stay above the splash of rain on the ground.
questions.onCorrect: A course 60 mm above the new ground is below the 150 mm guideline. Rain that splashes up the wall can get past it, so the patio should be lowered or fall away from the wall and stay clear of the course.

misconceptions.feedback: The course sits across the wall at a fixed height, and lowering it would put it closer to the damp. It is the ground that should stay below it.
It sits only 60 mm above it. The guideline is at least 150 mm, so rain splashing up the wall now reaches above the course.

acceptedIdeas: The course is only 60 mm above the ground, inside the splash zone
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The course is only 60 mm above the ground, inside the splash zone

choices.label: The course is only 60 mm above the ground, inside the splash zone
The course must be lowered by 90 mm to keep following the new ground level
Nothing, because the course still sits above the ground

questions.prompt: A client asks for the steepest roof possible on a 6 m span, 'for the best rain shedding'. Compare 30 and 45 degrees. What does the steeper roof cost?
hints: Work out the rise and the sloping width of each roof.
A steeper roof sheds water faster and gives more room beneath it. What does it need more of?
questions.onCorrect: At 45 degrees the ridge is 3.0 m above the eaves rather than 1.73 m, and each slope is 8.49 m wide rather than 6.93 m, so there is more room beneath and more to build.

misconceptions.feedback: The steeper roof has a taller ridge (3.0 m against 1.73 m) and a wider sloping surface (8.49 m against 6.93 m), so it needs more wall and more covering.
The flow depends on the plan area, which does not change with pitch. The gutters are the same size.

acceptedIdeas: It needs a taller ridge and more covering, in return for more room under the roof
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It needs a taller ridge and more covering, in return for more room under the roof

choices.label: It needs a taller ridge and more covering, in return for more room under the roof
It costs nothing extra, because pitch only changes the angle of the same materials
It reduces the flow the gutters must carry, so it saves on drainage

questions.prompt: A student multiplies the 30 mm by 50 and gets 1500 mm for the wall. What did the student overlook?
hints: Ask what the 50 percent print has done to every length on the sheet.
Halving every length on the sheet changes what 1 mm on the print stands for.

acceptedIdeas: The print is half-size, so its scale is now 1:100 and not the 1:50 shown
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The print is half-size, so its scale is now 1:100 and not the 1:50 shown

questions.onCorrect: Halving every length on the sheet doubles the ratio, so each millimetre on the print stands for 100 mm of wall, and 30 mm is 3000 mm.

choices.label: The print is half-size, so its scale is now 1:100 and not the 1:50 shown
A3 paper is a different shape from A1, so lengths on it are stretched
A print is never accurate, so the wall must be measured on the original sheet

misconceptions.feedback: A-series sheets all share one shape, so an even reduction shrinks every length by the same factor and nothing is stretched.
A print can be measured, and it reads correctly once its changed scale is used. The original sheet is not needed.

questions.prompt: The RIBA Plan of Work names the stages a building passes through, and drawings are issued at each, the early ones showing intent and the last ones giving instructions to build. In what order do these five come?
hints: A building cannot be built before it has been designed in detail.
Briefing comes before any design, and handover comes when the building is finished.
questions.onCorrect: Each stage's drawings build on the one before, and only the latest issue is used on site.

items: Strategic definition and briefing
Concept design
Technical design
Construction
Handover

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Strategic definition and briefing come first, then concept design, then technical design, then construction, and handover last. The early drawings show intent and the later ones give the builder instructions.

questions.prompt: A 47 × 245 mm joist would also pass the strength check. Why choose the 47 × 220 mm joist?
hints: Both joists pass. Ask what the extra depth costs.
Think about the timber used and the depth of the floor. Ask what you give up for strength you do not need.

acceptedIdeas: Both are strong enough, so the shallower joist is chosen to save timber
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both are strong enough, so the shallower joist is chosen to save timber

questions.onCorrect: Both joists pass, but the extra depth costs timber and raises the floor, so the shallower one that is strong enough is the one chosen.

choices.label: Joists deeper than 220 mm cannot be used at a 4 m span
Both are strong enough, so the shallower joist is chosen to save timber
The 245 mm joist is weaker, because a deeper joist always has a smaller Z value

misconceptions.feedback: Joists come in deeper sizes, and a deeper joist is stronger in bending. The span does not set a maximum depth.
Z grows with the square of the depth, so the deeper joist is the stronger one.

questions.prompt: The client asks for the south glazing to be doubled to 8 m². The glazing has U = 1.4 W/m²K. By how many watts does this raise the heating power the cabin needs when it is 20 K warmer inside than out?
hints: Only the added 4 m² of glass changes the total.
The extra loss rate is the added area times U.
Multiply that W/K figure by 20 K.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The extra 4 m² adds 4 × 1.4 = 5.6 W/K, and 5.6 × 20 = 112 W.

questions.onCorrect: The extra 112 W is the heat-loss side of the decision. The extra summer sun let in by the glass has to be checked as well, against the overhang and the depth rule.

misconceptions.feedback: 5.6 is the extra loss in W/K. Multiply by the 20 K difference to get watts.
224 W is the loss through all 8 m² of the doubled glazing. Only the extra 4 m² is added to the cabin’s loss.

questions.prompt: A client says the cabin would be cheaper to heat with the whole 14.4 m² south wall in glass, because sunshine is free. The glazing has U = 1.4 W/m²K and the wall U = 0.173, and the glazing is now 4 m². What do you tell them?
hints: Compare the heat lost per square metre of glass and of wall.
The sun helps only in daylight, and the glass loses heat all day and night.
questions.onCorrect: The extra 10.4 m² of glass replaces wall and adds 10.4 × (1.4 − 0.173) = 12.8 W/K, which is 255 W at 20 K. In June the same glass would admit more sun than the overhang shades.

misconceptions.feedback: Each square metre of glass loses 8 times as much as a square metre of wall, so the extra loss is not small.
They keep the weather out but not the heat in. Glass lets heat through far more easily than an insulated wall.

acceptedIdeas: It adds about 255 W of loss at 20 K, and the sun helps only when it shines
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It adds about 255 W of loss at 20 K, and the sun helps only when it shines

choices.label: It saves heat, since the sun is free and the extra loss is small
It makes no difference to the loss, since glass and wall both keep the weather out
It adds about 255 W of loss at 20 K, and the sun helps only when it shines

questions.prompt: In the cabin's wall, a concrete lintel crosses the insulation, so its inside face is colder than the wall around it. What is a place like this called?
hints: It is a place where a more conductive material crosses the insulation.
The name describes what the lintel does to the heat.
questions.onCorrect: A thermal bridge conducts heat better than the wall around it, so its inside face is colder and is where condensation or mould appears first. The fix is detailing that keeps the insulation continuous, since insulation elsewhere leaves the lintel cold.

misconceptions.feedback: The dew point belongs to the room air. The lintel is a place in the wall where heat passes more easily, and it is the first to fall below the dew point.
The U-value measures how much heat a wall lets through. The place where a conductive material breaks the insulation has its own name.

acceptedIdeas: thermal bridge
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: thermal bridge

questions.prompt: A cabin has 36 m² of wall at U = 0.173 W/m²K and 3 m² of glazing at U = 1.4. What percentage of the combined heat-loss rate UA of the two comes from the glazing, to the nearest whole percent?
hints: Work out UA for the wall and for the glazing separately.
Add them to get the combined UA.
Divide the glazing's UA by the combined UA.
questions.onCorrect: The glazing is under 8 percent of the area and causes 40 percent of the loss, which is why the size and quality of glazing are decided with the heat loss in view.

misconceptions.feedback: 8 percent is the glazing's share of the area. Its share of the heat loss is far higher, because glass conducts so much more readily.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Wall UA = 36 × 0.173 = 6.228 W/K; glazing UA = 3 × 1.4 = 4.2 W/K. Share = 4.2 ÷ 10.428 = 40.3 percent.

flashcards.front: Latitude 52. What is the noon sun altitude at the December solstice, in degrees to one decimal place?
The sun rises due east on which two dates?
flashcards.back: At the equinoxes the declination is zero, so the sun rises due east and sets due west.

acceptedIdeas: equinoxes
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: equinoxes

flashcards.front: Why does a fixed overhang over a south window help in both seasons?
flashcards.back: In June the sun is high, so the overhang shades the glass; in December the sun is low, so its shadow barely reaches the glass.

flashcards.front: Net area 85 m² at 85 percent efficiency. Gross area in m²?
What is the term for the list of spaces a building must provide, with their areas and relationships?
flashcards.back: The programme says what the building must contain before its form is chosen.

acceptedIdeas: programme
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: programme

flashcards.front: Why is net area never the same as the footprint?
flashcards.back: Walls, corridors, stairs and services need floor area that is not inside any room, so gross is larger than net.

flashcards.front: A room is 4.2 m wide. Its width on paper at 1:50 in millimetres?
Which view is a horizontal cut about 1.2 m above the floor?
flashcards.back: A floor plan cuts through walls, windows and doors so the rooms can be read.

acceptedIdeas: plan
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: plan

flashcards.front: What does 1:50 mean, and which way do you convert?
flashcards.back: 1 unit on paper stands for 50 in the building: multiply paper by 50 for real, divide real by 50 for paper.

flashcards.front: Riser 168.75 mm. What going does 2R + G = 630 give, in millimetres?
What is the name of the horizontal depth of one step?
flashcards.back: The going is the horizontal distance from one riser to the next.

acceptedIdeas: going
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: going

flashcards.front: Why is a steep stair a safety issue and not only a comfort one?
flashcards.back: A steep stair makes missteps and falls more likely, which is why codes limit the pitch as well as recommending a comfortable rule.

flashcards.front: Floor design load 2.925 kN/m² on joists at 0.4 m. Line load in kN/m?
What is the name for the continuous route that carries loads from the roof and floors to the ground?
flashcards.back: The load path must be unbroken, so every load has a member under it all the way to the ground.

acceptedIdeas: load path
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: load path

flashcards.front: Why is the area load multiplied by the joist spacing?
flashcards.back: Each joist carries a strip of floor as wide as the spacing, so kN per square metre times metres gives kN per metre.

flashcards.front: Indoors 150 lux, outdoors 10 000 lux. Daylight factor in percent?
In the depth rule L/W + L/Hw ≤ 2/(1 − R), what does R stand for?
flashcards.back: R is the average reflectance of the room’s surfaces, a number between 0 and 1.

acceptedIdeas: reflectance
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: reflectance

flashcards.front: Why is window area alone a poor measure of how well lit a room is?
flashcards.back: Where the window sits matters too: a higher window lights deeper, and the room’s depth and reflectances change how much reaches the back.

flashcards.front: Brick 102 mm, conductivity 0.77. Thermal resistance in m²K/W to 3 decimal places?
What do you do to the layer resistances and surface resistances to find the U-value?
flashcards.back: Add them and invert the total: U = 1 ÷ (Rsi + sum of R + Rse).

acceptedIdeas: add them and invert
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: add them and invert

flashcards.front: Why do insulation materials have low conductivity rather than great thickness being the key?
flashcards.back: Resistance is thickness divided by conductivity, so a layer with a conductivity 35 times lower resists 35 times more at the same thickness.

flashcards.front: V = 150 m³ at 0.5 air changes per hour. H = 0.33 n V in W/K?
What is the name for the temperature at which air of a given moisture content becomes saturated?
flashcards.back: Below the dew point, water condenses out of the air onto surfaces.

acceptedIdeas: dew point
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: dew point

flashcards.front: Why does an airtight house need deliberate ventilation?
flashcards.back: Without gaps, moisture and pollutants from people and cooking stay in, so fresh air must be supplied on purpose, ideally with heat recovery.

flashcards.front: 1 met is 58.2 W/m² and a person has 1.8 m² of skin. Heat at 1 met in watts to the nearest watt?
What is the average of the air temperature and the mean radiant temperature (at low air speed) called?
flashcards.back: Operative temperature approximates what a person feels, combining air and radiant temperature.

acceptedIdeas: operative temperature
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: operative temperature

flashcards.front: Name the three ways a body loses heat and which one a cold wall changes.
flashcards.back: Radiation, convection and evaporation; a cold wall increases radiation to it, so the room feels colder than the air temperature suggests.

flashcards.front: A 6 m span at 30 degrees. Ridge rise above the eaves in metres to 2 decimal places?
Which area of a roof decides how much rain reaches the gutters?
flashcards.back: Rain falls vertically, so the plan area, the area seen from above, is what the rain lands on.

acceptedIdeas: plan area
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: plan area

flashcards.front: Why must a damp-proof course stay above the ground, and not only stop rising damp?
flashcards.back: Rain splash and soil piled against the wall above the course carry water past it, so the course must clear the ground.

flashcards.front: A 12 m wall at 1:100. Length on paper in millimetres?
What are the thin lines with arrows that show lengths on a plan called?
flashcards.back: Dimension strings give lengths in tiers, so a builder can read each one without scaling the drawing.

acceptedIdeas: dimension strings
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: dimension strings

flashcards.front: Why are drawings called instructions and not pictures?
flashcards.back: They tell the builder what to build and, with the contract, define what the client has paid for, so they must be complete and to scale.

flashcards.front: 6 m × 4 m at 85 percent efficiency. Net area in m² to 1 decimal place?
What is the name for reducing heat loss through the building envelope before adding heating systems?
flashcards.back: Fabric first means insulating and sealing the envelope so that any heating system can be smaller.

acceptedIdeas: fabric first
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: fabric first

flashcards.front: Give one example of a decision in the cabin that affects another.
flashcards.back: The south glazing admits winter sun and daylight but adds heat loss and summer overheating, so its area is set by all three.
